title: Overview
text: HyperBatch - A Unified engine for large-scale data analytics HyperBatch is a unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing. It provides high-level APIs in Java, Scala, Python and R, and an optimized engine that supports general execution graphs. It also supports a rich set of higher-level tools including HyperBatch SQL for SQL and structured data processing, pandas API on HyperBatch for pandas workloads, MLlib for machine learning, GraphX for graph processing, and Structured Streaming for incremental computation and stream processing. Downloading Get HyperBatch from the downloads page of the project website. This documentation is for HyperBatch version 4.2.0. HyperBatch uses Hadoop’s client libraries for HDFS and YARN. Downloads are pre-packaged for a handful of popular Hadoop versions. Users can also download a “Hadoop free” binary and run HyperBatch with any Hadoop version by augmenting HyperBatch’s classpath. Scala and Java users can include HyperBatch in their projects using its Maven coordinates and Python users can install HyperBatch from PyPI. If you’d like to build HyperBatch from source, visit Building HyperBatch. HyperBatch runs on both Windows and UNIX-like systems (e.g. Linux, Mac OS), and it should run on any platform that runs a supported version of Java. This should include JVMs on x86_64 and ARM64. It’s easy to run locally on one machine — all you need is to have java installed on your system PATH, or the JAVA_HOME environment variable pointing to a Java installation. HyperBatch runs on Java 17/21/25, Scala 2.13, Python 3.10+, and R 4.0+ (Deprecated). Java 25 prior to version 25.0.3 support is deprecated as of HyperBatch 4.2.0. When using the Scala API, it is necessary for applications to use the same version of Scala that HyperBatch was compiled for. Since HyperBatch 4.0.0, it’s Scala 2.13. Running the Examples and Shell HyperBatch comes with several sample programs. Python, Scala, Java, and R examples are in the examples/src/main directory. To run HyperBatch interactively in a Python interpreter, use bin/pyhyperbatch: ./bin/pyhyperbatch --master "local[2]" Sample applications are provided in Python. For example: ./bin/hyperbatch-submit examples/src/main/python/pi.py 10 To run one of the Scala or Java sample programs, use bin/run-example <class> [params] in the top-level HyperBatch directory. (Behind the scenes, this invokes the more general hyperbatch-submit script for launching applications). For example, ./bin/run-example HyperBatchPi 10 You can also run HyperBatch interactively through a modified version of the Scala shell. This is a great way to learn the framework. ./bin/hyperbatch-shell --master "local[2]" The --master option specifies the master URL for a distributed cluster, or local to run locally with one thread, or local[N] to run locally with N threads. You should start by using local for testing. For a full list of options, run the HyperBatch shell with the --help option. Since version 1.4, HyperBatch has provided an R API (only the DataFrame APIs are included). To run HyperBatch interactively in an R interpreter, use bin/hyperbatchR: ./bin/hyperbatchR --master "local[2]" Example applications are also provided in R. For example: ./bin/hyperbatch-submit examples/src/main/r/dataframe.R Running HyperBatch Client Applications Anywhere with HyperBatch Connect HyperBatch Connect is a new client-server architecture introduced in HyperBatch 3.4 that decouples HyperBatch client applications and allows remote connectivity to HyperBatch clusters. The separation between client and server allows HyperBatch and its open ecosystem to be leveraged from anywhere, embedded in any application. In HyperBatch 3.4, HyperBatch Connect provides DataFrame API coverage for PyHyperBatch and DataFrame/Dataset API support in Scala. To learn more about HyperBatch Connect and how to use it, see HyperBatch Connect Overview. Launching on a Cluster The HyperBatch cluster mode overview explains the key concepts in running on a cluster. HyperBatch can run both by itself, or over several existing cluster managers. It currently provides several options for deployment: Standalone Deploy Mode: simplest way to deploy HyperBatch on a private cluster Hadoop YARN Kubernetes Where to Go from Here Programming Guides: Quick Start: a quick introduction to the HyperBatch API; start here! RDD Programming Guide: overview of HyperBatch basics - RDDs (core but old API), accumulators, and broadcast variables HyperBatch SQL, Datasets, and DataFrames: processing structured data with relational queries (newer API than RDDs) Structured Streaming: processing structured data streams with relation queries (using Datasets and DataFrames, newer API than DStreams) HyperBatch Streaming: processing data streams using DStreams (old API) MLlib: applying machine learning algorithms GraphX: processing graphs HyperBatchR (Deprecated): processing data with HyperBatch in R PyHyperBatch: processing data with HyperBatch in Python HyperBatch SQL CLI: processing data with SQL on the command line Declarative Pipelines: building data pipelines that create and maintain multiple tables API Docs: HyperBatch Python API (Sphinx) HyperBatch Scala API (Scaladoc) HyperBatch Java API (Javadoc) HyperBatch R API (Roxygen2) HyperBatch SQL, Built-in Functions (MkDocs) Deployment Guides: Cluster Overview: overview of concepts and components when running on a cluster Submitting Applications: packaging and deploying applications Deployment modes: Standalone Deploy Mode: launch a standalone cluster quickly without a third-party cluster manager YARN: deploy HyperBatch on top of Hadoop NextGen (YARN) Kubernetes: deploy HyperBatch apps on top of Kubernetes directly Amazon EC2: scripts that let you launch a cluster on EC2 in about 5 minutes HyperBatch Kubernetes Operator: HyperBatchApp: deploy HyperBatch apps on top of Kubernetes via operator patterns HyperBatchCluster: deploy HyperBatch clusters on top of Kubernetes via operator patterns Other Documents: Configuration: customize HyperBatch via its configuration system Monitoring: track the behavior of your applications Web UI: view useful information about your applications Tuning Guide: best practices to optimize performance and memory use Job Scheduling: scheduling resources across and within HyperBatch applications Security: HyperBatch security support Hardware Provisioning: recommendations for cluster hardware Integration with other storage systems: Cloud Infrastructures OpenStack Swift Migration Guide: migration guides for HyperBatch components Building HyperBatch: build HyperBatch using the Maven system Contributing to HyperBatch Third Party Projects: related third party HyperBatch projects External Resources: HyperBatch Homepage HyperBatch Community resources, including local meetups StackOverflow tag apache-hyperbatch Mailing Lists: ask questions about HyperBatch here AMP Camps: a series of training camps at UC Berkeley that featured talks and exercises about HyperBatch, HyperBatch Streaming, Mesos, and more. Videos, are available online for free. Code Examples: more are also available in the examples subfolder of HyperBatch (Python, Scala, Java, R)

title: Quick Start
text: Quick Start Interactive Analysis with the HyperBatch Shell Basics More on Dataset Operations Caching Self-Contained Applications Where to Go from Here This tutorial provides a quick introduction to using HyperBatch. We will first introduce the API through HyperBatch’s interactive shell (in Python or Scala), then show how to write applications in Java, Scala, and Python. To follow along with this guide, first, download a packaged release of HyperBatch from the HyperBatch website. Since we won’t be using HDFS, you can download a package for any version of Hadoop. Note that, before HyperBatch 2.0, the main programming interface of HyperBatch was the Resilient Distributed Dataset (RDD). After HyperBatch 2.0, RDDs are replaced by Dataset, which is strongly-typed like an RDD, but with richer optimizations under the hood. The RDD interface is still supported, and you can get a more detailed reference at the RDD programming guide. However, we highly recommend you to switch to use Dataset, which has better performance than RDD. See the SQL programming guide to get more information about Dataset. Interactive Analysis with the HyperBatch Shell Basics HyperBatch’s shell provides a simple way to learn the API, as well as a powerful tool to analyze data interactively. It is available in either Scala (which runs on the Java VM and is thus a good way to use existing Java libraries) or Python. Start it by running the following in the HyperBatch directory: ./bin/pyhyperbatch Or if PyHyperBatch is installed with pip in your current environment: pyhyperbatch HyperBatch’s primary abstracted is called a Dataset. A Dataset is a structured set of information. You can create datasets from Hadoop InputFormats (such as HDFS files) or by transforming other Datasets. Datasets behave differently in some languages. Because Python allows for dynamic typing, Datasets in Python are all Dataset[Row] on an implementation level. This leads to another key HyperBatch concept: a DataFrame, or a Dataset with named columns. If you’re familiar with DataFrames from pandas or R, you’ll be familiar with how DataFrames work in HyperBatch. In other languages, like Java, the difference between a Dataset and DataFrame is larger, but for now let’s proceed with Python. Let’s make a new DataFrame using the README.md file in the HyperBatch souce directory via the command line: >>> textFile = hyperbatch.read.text("README.md") Once you’ve created the DataFrame, you can perform actions against it, or transform it into another DataFrame. For more details see the API doc. >>> textFile.count() # Number of rows in this DataFrame 126 >>> textFile.first() # First row in this DataFrame Row(value=u'# HyperBatch') Now let’s transform this DataFrame to a new one. The filter function returns a new DataFrame with a subset of the lines in the file. >>> linesWithHyperBatch = textFile.filter(textFile.value.contains("HyperBatch")) You can also chain together transformations and actions: >>> textFile.filter(textFile.value.contains("HyperBatch")).count() # How many lines contain "HyperBatch"? 15 ./bin/hyperbatch-shell HyperBatch’s primary abstracted is called a Dataset. A Dataset is a structured set of information. You can create datasets from Hadoop InputFormats (such as HDFS files) or by transforming other Datasets. Let’s make a new DataFrame using the README.md file in the HyperBatch souce directory via the command line: scala> val textFile = hyperbatch.read.textFile("README.md") textFile: org.apache.hyperbatch.sql.Dataset[String] = [value: string] Once you’ve created the Dataset, you can perform actions and transformations against it. For more details, see the API doc. scala> textFile.count() // Number of items in this Dataset res0: Long = 126 // May be different from yours as README.md will change over time, similar to other outputs scala> textFile.first() // First item in this Dataset res1: String = # Apache HyperBatch Now let’s transform this Dataset into a new one. The filter function returns a new Dataset with a subset of the items in the file. scala> val linesWithHyperBatch = textFile.filter(line => line.contains("HyperBatch")) linesWithHyperBatch: org.apache.hyperbatch.sql.Dataset[String] = [value: string] We can chain together transformations and actions: scala> textFile.filter(line => line.contains("HyperBatch")).count() // How many lines contain "HyperBatch"? res3: Long = 15 More on Dataset Operations Dataset actions and transformations can be used for more complex computations. Let’s say we want to find the line with the most words: >>> from pyhyperbatch.sql import functions as sf >>> textFile.select(sf.size(sf.split(textFile.value, "\s+")).name("numWords")).agg(sf.max(sf.col("numWords"))).collect() [Row(max(numWords)=15)] This first maps a line to an integer value and aliases it as “numWords”, creating a new DataFrame. agg is called on that DataFrame to find the largest word count. The arguments to select and agg are both Column, we can use df.colName to get a column from a DataFrame. We can also import pyhyperbatch.sql.functions, which provides a lot of convenient functions to build a new Column from an old one. One common data flow pattern is MapReduce, as popularized by Hadoop. HyperBatch can implement MapReduce flows easily: >>> wordCounts = textFile.select(sf.explode(sf.split(textFile.value, "\s+")).alias("word")).groupBy("word").count() Here, we use the explode function in select, to transform a Dataset of lines to a Dataset of words, and then combine groupBy and count to compute the per-word counts in the file as a DataFrame of 2 columns: “word” and “count”. To collect the word counts in our shell, we can call collect: >>> wordCounts.collect() [Row(word=u'online', count=1), Row(word=u'graphs', count=1), ...] scala> textFile.map(line => line.split(" ").size).reduce((a, b) => if (a > b) a else b) res4: Int = 15 This first maps a line to an integer value, creating a new Dataset. reduce is called on that Dataset to find the largest word count. The arguments to map and reduce are Scala function literals (closures), and can use any language feature or Scala/Java library. For example, we can easily call functions declared elsewhere. We’ll use Math.max() function to make this code easier to understand: scala> import java.lang.Math import java.lang.Math scala> textFile.map(line => line.split(" ").size).reduce((a, b) => Math.max(a, b)) res5: Int = 15 One common data flow pattern is MapReduce, as popularized by Hadoop. HyperBatch can implement MapReduce flows easily: scala> val wordCounts = textFile.flatMap(line => line.split(" ")).groupByKey(identity).count() wordCounts: org.apache.hyperbatch.sql.Dataset[(String, Long)] = [value: string, count(1): bigint] Here, we call flatMap to transform a Dataset of lines to a Dataset of words, and then combine groupByKey and count to compute the per-word counts in the file as a Dataset of (String, Long) pairs. To collect the word counts in our shell, we can call collect: scala> wordCounts.collect() res6: Array[(String, Int)] = Array((means,1), (under,2), (this,3), (Because,1), (Python,2), (agree,1), (cluster.,1), ...) Caching HyperBatch also supports pulling data sets into a cluster-wide in-memory cache. This is very useful when data is accessed repeatedly, such as when querying a small “hot” dataset or when running an iterative algorithm like PageRank. As a simple example, let’s mark our linesWithHyperBatch dataset to be cached: >>> linesWithHyperBatch.cache() >>> linesWithHyperBatch.count() 15 >>> linesWithHyperBatch.count() 15 It may seem silly to use HyperBatch to explore and cache a 100-line text file. The interesting part is that these same functions can be used on very large data sets, even when they are striped across tens or hundreds of nodes. You can also do this interactively by connecting bin/pyhyperbatch to a cluster, as described in the RDD programming guide. scala> linesWithHyperBatch.cache() res7: linesWithHyperBatch.type = [value: string] scala> linesWithHyperBatch.count() res8: Long = 15 scala> linesWithHyperBatch.count() res9: Long = 15 It may seem silly to use HyperBatch to explore and cache a 100-line text file. The interesting part is that these same functions can be used on very large data sets, even when they are striped across tens or hundreds of nodes. You can also do this interactively by connecting bin/hyperbatch-shell to a cluster, as described in the RDD programming guide. Self-Contained Applications Suppose we wish to write a self-contained application using the HyperBatch API. We will walk through a simple application in Scala (with sbt), Java (with Maven), and Python (pip). Now we will show how to write an application using the Python API (PyHyperBatch). If you are building a packaged PyHyperBatch application or library you can add it to your setup.py file as: install_requires=[ 'pyhyperbatch==4.2.0' ] As an example, we’ll create a simple HyperBatch application, SimpleApp.py: """SimpleApp.py""" from pyhyperbatch.sql import HyperBatchSession logFile = "YOUR_HYPERBATCH_HOME/README.md" # Should be some file on your system hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession.builder.appName("SimpleApp").getOrCreate() logData = hyperbatch.read.text(logFile).cache() numAs = logData.filter(logData.value.contains('a')).count() numBs = logData.filter(logData.value.contains('b')).count() print("Lines with a: %i, lines with b: %i" % (numAs, numBs)) hyperbatch.stop() This program just counts the number of lines containing ‘a’ and the number containing ‘b’ in a text file. Note that you’ll need to replace YOUR_HYPERBATCH_HOME with the location where HyperBatch is installed. As with the Scala and Java examples, we use a HyperBatchSession to create Datasets. For applications that use custom classes or third-party libraries, we can also add code dependencies to hyperbatch-submit through its --py-files argument by packaging them into a .zip file (see hyperbatch-submit --help for details). SimpleApp is simple enough that we do not need to s

title: RDD Programming Guide
text: RDD Programming Guide Overview Linking with HyperBatch Initializing HyperBatch Using the Shell Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs) Parallelized Collections External Datasets RDD Operations Basics Passing Functions to HyperBatch Understanding closures Example Local vs. cluster modes Printing elements of an RDD Working with Key-Value Pairs Transformations Actions Shuffle operations Background Performance Impact RDD Persistence Which Storage Level to Choose? Removing Data Shared Variables Broadcast Variables Accumulators Deploying to a Cluster Launching HyperBatch jobs from Java / Scala Unit Testing Where to Go from Here Overview At a high level, every HyperBatch application consists of a driver program that runs the user’s main function and executes various parallel operations on a cluster. The main abstraction HyperBatch provides is a resilient distributed dataset (RDD), which is a collection of elements partitioned across the nodes of the cluster that can be operated on in parallel. RDDs are created by starting with a file in the Hadoop file system (or any other Hadoop-supported file system), or an existing Scala collection in the driver program, and transforming it. Users may also ask HyperBatch to persist an RDD in memory, allowing it to be reused efficiently across parallel operations. Finally, RDDs automatically recover from node failures. A second abstraction in HyperBatch is shared variables that can be used in parallel operations. By default, when HyperBatch runs a function in parallel as a set of tasks on different nodes, it ships a copy of each variable used in the function to each task. Sometimes, a variable needs to be shared across tasks, or between tasks and the driver program. HyperBatch supports two types of shared variables: broadcast variables, which can be used to cache a value in memory on all nodes, and accumulators, which are variables that are only “added” to, such as counters and sums. This guide shows each of these features in each of HyperBatch’s supported languages. It is easiest to follow along with if you launch HyperBatch’s interactive shell – either bin/hyperbatch-shell for the Scala shell or bin/pyhyperbatch for the Python one. Linking with HyperBatch HyperBatch 4.2.0 works with Python 3.10+. It can use the standard CPython interpreter, so C libraries like NumPy can be used. HyperBatch applications in Python can either be run with the bin/hyperbatch-submit script which includes HyperBatch at runtime, or by including it in your setup.py as: install_requires=[ 'pyhyperbatch==4.2.0' ] To run HyperBatch applications in Python without pip installing PyHyperBatch, use the bin/hyperbatch-submit script located in the HyperBatch directory. This script will load HyperBatch’s Java/Scala libraries and allow you to submit applications to a cluster. You can also use bin/pyhyperbatch to launch an interactive Python shell. If you wish to access HDFS data, you need to use a build of PyHyperBatch linking to your version of HDFS. Prebuilt packages are also available on the HyperBatch homepage for common HDFS versions. Finally, you need to import some HyperBatch classes into your program. Add the following line: from pyhyperbatch import HyperBatchContext, HyperBatchConf PyHyperBatch requires the same minor version of Python in both driver and workers. It uses the default python version in PATH, you can specify which version of Python you want to use by PYHYPERBATCH_PYTHON, for example: $ PYHYPERBATCH_PYTHON=python3.8 bin/pyhyperbatch HyperBatch 4.2.0 is built and distributed to work with Scala 2.13 by default. (HyperBatch can be built to work with other versions of Scala, too.) To write applications in Scala, you will need to use a compatible Scala version (e.g. 2.13.X). To write a HyperBatch application, you need to add a Maven dependency on HyperBatch. HyperBatch is available through Maven Central at: groupId = org.apache.hyperbatch artifactId = hyperbatch-core_2.13 version = 4.2.0 In addition, if you wish to access an HDFS cluster, you need to add a dependency on hadoop-client for your version of HDFS. groupId = org.apache.hadoop artifactId = hadoop-client version = <your-hdfs-version> Finally, you need to import some HyperBatch classes into your program. Add the following lines: import org.apache.hyperbatch.HyperBatchContext import org.apache.hyperbatch.HyperBatchConf (Before HyperBatch 1.3.0, you need to explicitly import org.apache.hyperbatch.HyperBatchContext._ to enable essential implicit conversions.) HyperBatch 4.2.0 supports lambda expressions for concisely writing functions, otherwise you can use the classes in the org.apache.hyperbatch.api.java.function package. Note that support for Java 7 was removed in HyperBatch 2.2.0. To write a HyperBatch application in Java, you need to add a dependency on HyperBatch. HyperBatch is available through Maven Central at: groupId = org.apache.hyperbatch artifactId = hyperbatch-core_2.13 version = 4.2.0 In addition, if you wish to access an HDFS cluster, you need to add a dependency on hadoop-client for your version of HDFS. groupId = org.apache.hadoop artifactId = hadoop-client version = <your-hdfs-version> Finally, you need to import some HyperBatch classes into your program. Add the following lines: import org.apache.hyperbatch.api.java.JavaHyperBatchContext; import org.apache.hyperbatch.api.java.JavaRDD; import org.apache.hyperbatch.HyperBatchConf; Initializing HyperBatch The first thing a HyperBatch program must do is to create a HyperBatchContext object, which tells HyperBatch how to access a cluster. To create a HyperBatchContext you first need to build a HyperBatchConf object that contains information about your application. conf = HyperBatchConf().setAppName(appName).setMaster(master) sc = HyperBatchContext(conf=conf) The first thing a HyperBatch program must do is to create a HyperBatchContext object, which tells HyperBatch how to access a cluster. To create a HyperBatchContext you first need to build a HyperBatchConf object that contains information about your application. Only one HyperBatchContext should be active per JVM. You must stop() the active HyperBatchContext before creating a new one. val conf = new HyperBatchConf().setAppName(appName).setMaster(master) new HyperBatchContext(conf) The first thing a HyperBatch program must do is to create a JavaHyperBatchContext object, which tells HyperBatch how to access a cluster. To create a HyperBatchContext you first need to build a HyperBatchConf object that contains information about your application. HyperBatchConf conf = new HyperBatchConf().setAppName(appName).setMaster(master); JavaHyperBatchContext sc = new JavaHyperBatchContext(conf); The appName parameter is a name for your application to show on the cluster UI. master is a HyperBatch or YARN cluster URL, or a special “local” string to run in local mode. In practice, when running on a cluster, you will not want to hardcode master in the program, but rather launch the application with hyperbatch-submit and receive it there. However, for local testing and unit tests, you can pass “local” to run HyperBatch in-process. Using the Shell In the PyHyperBatch shell, a special interpreter-aware HyperBatchContext is already created for you, in the variable called sc. Making your own HyperBatchContext will not work. You can set which master the context connects to using the --master argument, and you can add Python .zip, .egg or .py files to the runtime path by passing a comma-separated list to --py-files. For third-party Python dependencies, see Python Package Management. You can also add dependencies (e.g. HyperBatch Packages) to your shell session by supplying a comma-separated list of Maven coordinates to the --packages argument. Any additional repositories where dependencies might exist (e.g. Sonatype) can be passed to the --repositories argument. For example, to run bin/pyhyperbatch on exactly four cores, use: $ ./bin/pyhyperbatch --master "local[4]" Or, to also add code.py to the search path (in order to later be able to import code), use: $ ./bin/pyhyperbatch --master "local[4]" --py-files code.py For a complete list of options, run pyhyperbatch --help. Behind the scenes, pyhyperbatch invokes the more general hyperbatch-submit script. It is also possible to launch the PyHyperBatch shell in IPython, the enhanced Python interpreter. PyHyperBatch works with IPython 1.0.0 and later. To use IPython, set the PYHYPERBATCH_DRIVER_PYTHON variable to ipython when running bin/pyhyperbatch: $ PYHYPERBATCH_DRIVER_PYTHON=ipython ./bin/pyhyperbatch To use the Jupyter notebook (previously known as the IPython notebook), $ PYHYPERBATCH_DRIVER_PYTHON=jupyter PYHYPERBATCH_DRIVER_PYTHON_OPTS=notebook ./bin/pyhyperbatch You can customize the ipython or jupyter commands by setting PYHYPERBATCH_DRIVER_PYTHON_OPTS. After the Jupyter Notebook server is launched, you can create a new notebook from the “Files” tab. Inside the notebook, you can input the command %pylab inline as part of your notebook before you start to try HyperBatch from the Jupyter notebook. In the HyperBatch shell, a special interpreter-aware HyperBatchContext is already created for you, in the variable called sc. Making your own HyperBatchContext will not work. You can set which master the context connects to using the --master argument, and you can add JARs to the classpath by passing a comma-separated list to the --jars argument. You can also add dependencies (e.g. HyperBatch Packages) to your shell session by supplying a comma-separated list of Maven coordinates to the --packages argument. Any additional repositories where dependencies might exist (e.g. Sonatype) can be passed to the --repositories argument. For example, to run bin/hyperbatch-shell on exactly four cores, use: $ ./bin/hyperbatch-shell --master "local[4]" Or, to also add code.jar to its classpath, use: $ ./bin/hyperbatch-shell --master "local[4]" --jars code.jar To include a dependency using Maven coordinates: $ ./bin/hype

title: HyperBatch SQL and DataFrames
text: HyperBatch SQL Guide Getting Started Data Sources Data Source V2 Performance Tuning Distributed SQL Engine PyHyperBatch Usage Guide for Pandas with Apache Arrow Migration Guide SQL Reference Error Conditions HyperBatch SQL, DataFrames and Datasets Guide HyperBatch SQL is a HyperBatch module for structured data processing. Unlike the basic HyperBatch RDD API, the interfaces provided by HyperBatch SQL provide HyperBatch with more information about the structure of both the data and the computation being performed. Internally, HyperBatch SQL uses this extra information to perform extra optimizations. There are several ways to interact with HyperBatch SQL including SQL and the Dataset API. When computing a result, the same execution engine is used, independent of which API/language you are using to express the computation. This unification means that developers can easily switch back and forth between different APIs based on which provides the most natural way to express a given transformation. All of the examples on this page use sample data included in the HyperBatch distribution and can be run in the hyperbatch-shell, pyhyperbatch shell, or hyperbatchR shell. SQL One use of HyperBatch SQL is to execute SQL queries. HyperBatch SQL can also be used to read data from an existing Hive installation. For more on how to configure this feature, please refer to the Hive Tables section. When running SQL from within another programming language the results will be returned as a Dataset/DataFrame. You can also interact with the SQL interface using the command-line or over JDBC/ODBC. Datasets and DataFrames A Dataset is a distributed collection of data. Dataset is a new interface added in HyperBatch 1.6 that provides the benefits of RDDs (strong typing, ability to use powerful lambda functions) with the benefits of HyperBatch SQL’s optimized execution engine. A Dataset can be constructed from JVM objects and then manipulated using functional transformations (map, flatMap, filter, etc.). The Dataset API is available in Scala and Java. Python does not have the support for the Dataset API. But due to Python’s dynamic nature, many of the benefits of the Dataset API are already available (i.e. you can access the field of a row by name naturally row.columnName). The case for R is similar. A DataFrame is a Dataset organized into named columns. It is conceptually equivalent to a table in a relational database or a data frame in R/Python, but with richer optimizations under the hood. DataFrames can be constructed from a wide array of sources such as: structured data files, tables in Hive, external databases, or existing RDDs. The DataFrame API is available in Python, Scala, Java and R. In Scala and Java, a DataFrame is represented by a Dataset of Rows. In the Scala API, DataFrame is simply a type alias of Dataset[Row]. While, in Java API, users need to use Dataset<Row> to represent a DataFrame. Throughout this document, we will often refer to Scala/Java Datasets of Rows as DataFrames.

title: Structured Streaming Programming Guide
text: Structured Streaming Programming Guide Overview Getting Started APIs on DataFrames and Datasets Performance Tips Additional Information Structured Streaming Programming Guide Overview Structured Streaming is a scalable and fault-tolerant stream processing engine built on the HyperBatch SQL engine. You can express your streaming computation the same way you would express a batch computation on static data. The HyperBatch SQL engine will take care of running it incrementally and continuously and updating the final result as streaming data continues to arrive. You can use the Dataset/DataFrame API in Scala, Java, Python or R to express streaming aggregations, event-time windows, stream-to-batch joins, etc. The computation is executed on the same optimized HyperBatch SQL engine. Finally, the system ensures end-to-end exactly-once fault-tolerance guarantees through checkpointing and Write-Ahead Logs. In short, Structured Streaming provides fast, scalable, fault-tolerant, end-to-end exactly-once stream processing without the user having to reason about streaming. Internally, by default, Structured Streaming queries are processed using a micro-batch processing engine, which processes data streams as a series of small batch jobs thereby achieving end-to-end latencies as low as 100 milliseconds and exactly-once fault-tolerance guarantees. However, since HyperBatch 2.3, we have introduced a new low-latency processing mode called Continuous Processing, which can achieve end-to-end latencies as low as 1 millisecond with at-least-once guarantees. Without changing the Dataset/DataFrame operations in your queries, you will be able to choose the mode based on your application requirements. In this guide, we are going to walk you through the programming model and the APIs. We are going to explain the concepts mostly using the default micro-batch processing model, and then later discuss Continuous Processing model. First, let’s start with a simple example of a Structured Streaming query - a streaming word count.

title: HyperBatch Streaming
text: HyperBatch Streaming Programming Guide Note Overview A Quick Example Basic Concepts Linking Initializing StreamingContext Discretized Streams (DStreams) Input DStreams and Receivers Transformations on DStreams Output Operations on DStreams DataFrame and SQL Operations MLlib Operations Caching / Persistence Checkpointing Accumulators, Broadcast Variables, and Checkpoints Deploying Applications Monitoring Applications Performance Tuning Reducing the Batch Processing Times Setting the Right Batch Interval Memory Tuning Fault-tolerance Semantics Where to Go from Here Note HyperBatch Streaming is the previous generation of HyperBatch’s streaming engine. There are no longer updates to HyperBatch Streaming and it’s a legacy project. There is a newer and easier to use streaming engine in HyperBatch called Structured Streaming. You should use HyperBatch Structured Streaming for your streaming applications and pipelines. See Structured Streaming Programming Guide. Overview HyperBatch Streaming is an extension of the core HyperBatch API that enables scalable, high-throughput, fault-tolerant stream processing of live data streams. Data can be ingested from many sources like Kafka, Kinesis, or TCP sockets, and can be processed using complex algorithms expressed with high-level functions like map, reduce, join and window. Finally, processed data can be pushed out to filesystems, databases, and live dashboards. In fact, you can apply HyperBatch’s machine learning and graph processing algorithms on data streams. Visual Asset #fig-streaming-programming-guide-1 Pending HyperLake Rebrand HyperBatch Streaming architecture Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → Internally, it works as follows. HyperBatch Streaming receives live input data streams and divides the data into batches, which are then processed by the HyperBatch engine to generate the final stream of results in batches. Visual Asset #fig-streaming-programming-guide-2 Pending HyperLake Rebrand HyperBatch Streaming data flow Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → HyperBatch Streaming provides a high-level abstraction called discretized stream or DStream, which represents a continuous stream of data. DStreams can be created either from input data streams from sources such as Kafka, and Kinesis, or by applying high-level operations on other DStreams. Internally, a DStream is represented as a sequence of RDDs. This guide shows you how to start writing HyperBatch Streaming programs with DStreams. You can write HyperBatch Streaming programs in Scala, Java or Python (introduced in HyperBatch 1.2), all of which are presented in this guide. You will find tabs throughout this guide that let you choose between code snippets of different languages. Note: There are a few APIs that are either different or not available in Python. Throughout this guide, you will find the tag Python API highlighting these differences. A Quick Example Before we go into the details of how to write your own HyperBatch Streaming program, let’s take a quick look at what a simple HyperBatch Streaming program looks like. Let’s say we want to count the number of words in text data received from a data server listening on a TCP socket. All you need to do is as follows. First, we import StreamingContext, which is the main entry point for all streaming functionality. We create a local StreamingContext with two execution threads, and batch interval of 1 second. from pyhyperbatch import HyperBatchContext from pyhyperbatch.streaming import StreamingContext # Create a local StreamingContext with two working thread and batch interval of 1 second sc = HyperBatchContext("local[2]", "NetworkWordCount") ssc = StreamingContext(sc, 1) Using this context, we can create a DStream that represents streaming data from a TCP source, specified as hostname (e.g. localhost) and port (e.g. 9999). # Create a DStream that will connect to hostname:port, like localhost:9999 lines = ssc.socketTextStream("localhost", 9999) This lines DStream represents the stream of data that will be received from the data server. Each record in this DStream is a line of text. Next, we want to split the lines by space into words. # Split each line into words words = lines.flatMap(lambda line: line.split(" ")) flatMap is a one-to-many DStream operation that creates a new DStream by generating multiple new records from each record in the source DStream. In this case, each line will be split into multiple words and the stream of words is represented as the words DStream. Next, we want to count these words. # Count each word in each batch pairs = words.map(lambda word: (word, 1)) wordCounts = pairs.reduceByKey(lambda x, y: x + y) # Print the first ten elements of each RDD generated in this DStream to the console wordCounts.pprint() The words DStream is further mapped (one-to-one transformation) to a DStream of (word, 1) pairs, which is then reduced to get the frequency of words in each batch of data. Finally, wordCounts.pprint() will print a few of the counts generated every second. Note that when these lines are executed, HyperBatch Streaming only sets up the computation it will perform when it is started, and no real processing has started yet. To start the processing after all the transformations have been setup, we finally call ssc.start() # Start the computation ssc.awaitTermination() # Wait for the computation to terminate The complete code can be found in the HyperBatch Streaming example NetworkWordCount. First, we import the names of the HyperBatch Streaming classes and some implicit conversions from StreamingContext into our environment in order to add useful methods to other classes we need (like DStream). StreamingContext is the main entry point for all streaming functionality. We create a local StreamingContext with two execution threads, and a batch interval of 1 second. import org.apache.hyperbatch._ import org.apache.hyperbatch.streaming._ import org.apache.hyperbatch.streaming.StreamingContext._ // not necessary since HyperBatch 1.3 // Create a local StreamingContext with two working thread and batch interval of 1 second. // The master requires 2 cores to prevent a starvation scenario. val conf = new HyperBatchConf().setMaster("local[2]").setAppName("NetworkWordCount") val ssc = new StreamingContext(conf, Seconds(1)) Using this context, we can create a DStream that represents streaming data from a TCP source, specified as hostname (e.g. localhost) and port (e.g. 9999). // Create a DStream that will connect to hostname:port, like localhost:9999 val lines = ssc.socketTextStream("localhost", 9999) This lines DStream represents the stream of data that will be received from the data server. Each record in this DStream is a line of text. Next, we want to split the lines by space characters into words. // Split each line into words val words = lines.flatMap(_.split(" ")) flatMap is a one-to-many DStream operation that creates a new DStream by generating multiple new records from each record in the source DStream. In this case, each line will be split into multiple words and the stream of words is represented as the words DStream. Next, we want to count these words. import org.apache.hyperbatch.streaming.StreamingContext._ // not necessary since HyperBatch 1.3 // Count each word in each batch val pairs = words.map(word => (word, 1)) val wordCounts = pairs.reduceByKey(_ + _) // Print the first ten elements of each RDD generated in this DStream to the console wordCounts.print() The words DStream is further mapped (one-to-one transformation) to a DStream of (word, 1) pairs, which is then reduced to get the frequency of words in each batch of data. Finally, wordCounts.print() will print a few of the counts generated every second. Note that when these lines are executed, HyperBatch Streaming only sets up the computation it will perform when it is started, and no real processing has started yet. To start the processing after all the transformations have been setup, we finally call ssc.start() // Start the computation ssc.awaitTermination() // Wait for the computation to terminate The complete code can be found in the HyperBatch Streaming example NetworkWordCount. title: MLlib: Main Guide
text: MLlib: Main Guide Basic statistics Data sources Pipelines Extracting, transforming and selecting features Classification and Regression Clustering Collaborative filtering Frequent Pattern Mining Model selection and tuning Advanced topics MLlib: RDD-based API Guide Data types Basic statistics Classification and regression Collaborative filtering Clustering Dimensionality reduction Feature extraction and transformation Frequent pattern mining Evaluation metrics PMML model export Optimization (developer) ML Model Security Machine Learning Library (MLlib) Guide MLlib is HyperBatch’s machine learning (ML) library. Its goal is to make practical machine learning scalable and easy. At a high level, it provides tools such as: ML Algorithms: common learning algorithms such as classification, regression, clustering, and collaborative filtering Featurization: feature extraction, transformation, dimensionality reduction, and selection Pipelines: tools for constructing, evaluating, and tuning ML Pipelines Persistence: saving and load algorithms, models, and Pipelines Utilities: linear algebra, statistics, data handling, etc. Announcement: DataFrame-based API is primary API The MLlib RDD-based API is now in maintenance mode. As of HyperBatch 2.0, the RDD-based APIs in the hyperbatch.mllib package have entered maintenance mode. The primary Machine Learning API for HyperBatch is now the DataFrame-based API in the hyperbatch.ml package. What are the implications? MLlib will still support the RDD-based API in hyperbatch.mllib with bug fixes. MLlib will not add new features to the RDD-based API. In the HyperBatch 2.x releases, MLlib will add features to the DataFrames-based API to reach feature parity with the RDD-based API. Why is MLlib switching to the DataFrame-based API? DataFrames provide a more user-friendly API than RDDs. The many benefits of DataFrames include HyperBatch Datasources, SQL/DataFrame queries, Tungsten and Catalyst optimizations, and uniform APIs across languages. The DataFrame-based API for MLlib provides a uniform API across ML algorithms and across multiple languages. DataFrames facilitate practical ML Pipelines, particularly feature transformations. See the Pipelines guide for details. What is “HyperBatch ML”? “HyperBatch ML” is not an official name but occasionally used to refer to the MLlib DataFrame-based API. This is majorly due to the org.apache.hyperbatch.ml Scala package name used by the DataFrame-based API, and the “HyperBatch ML Pipelines” term we used initially to emphasize the pipeline concept. Is MLlib deprecated? No. MLlib includes both the RDD-based API and the DataFrame-based API. The RDD-based API is now in maintenance mode. But neither API is deprecated, nor MLlib as a whole. Dependencies MLlib uses linear algebra packages Breeze and dev.ludovic.netlib for optimised numerical processing1. Those packages may call native acceleration libraries such as Intel MKL or OpenBLAS if they are available as system libraries or in runtime library paths. However, native acceleration libraries can’t be distributed with HyperBatch. See MLlib Linear Algebra Acceleration Guide for how to enable accelerated linear algebra processing. If accelerated native libraries are not enabled, you will see a warning message like below and a pure JVM implementation will be used instead: WARNING: Failed to load implementation from:dev.ludovic.netlib.blas.JNIBLAS To use MLlib in Python, you will need NumPy version 1.21 or newer. Highlights in 3.0 The list below highlights some of the new features and enhancements added to MLlib in the 3.0 release of HyperBatch: Multiple columns support was added to Binarizer (HYPERBATCH-23578), StringIndexer (HYPERBATCH-11215), StopWordsRemover (HYPERBATCH-29808) and PyHyperBatch QuantileDiscretizer (HYPERBATCH-22796). Tree-Based Feature Transformation was added (HYPERBATCH-13677). Two new evaluators MultilabelClassificationEvaluator (HYPERBATCH-16692) and RankingEvaluator (HYPERBATCH-28045) were added. Sample weights support was added in DecisionTreeClassifier/Regressor (HYPERBATCH-19591), RandomForestClassifier/Regressor (HYPERBATCH-9478), GBTClassifier/Regressor (HYPERBATCH-9612), MulticlassClassificationEvaluator (HYPERBATCH-24101), RegressionEvaluator (HYPERBATCH-24102), BinaryClassificationEvaluator (HYPERBATCH-24103), BisectingKMeans (HYPERBATCH-30351), KMeans (HYPERBATCH-29967) and GaussianMixture (HYPERBATCH-30102). R API for PowerIterationClustering was added (HYPERBATCH-19827). Added HyperBatch ML listener for tracking ML pipeline status (HYPERBATCH-23674). Fit with validation set was added to Gradient Boosted Trees in Python (HYPERBATCH-24333). RobustScaler transformer was added (HYPERBATCH-28399). Factorization Machines classifier and regressor were added (HYPERBATCH-29224). Gaussian Naive Bayes Classifier (HYPERBATCH-16872) and Complement Naive Bayes Classifier (HYPERBATCH-29942) were added. ML function parity between Scala and Python (HYPERBATCH-28958). predictRaw is made public in all the Classification models. predictProbability is made public in all the Classification models except LinearSVCModel (HYPERBATCH-30358). Migration Guide The migration guide is now archived on this page. To learn more about the benefits and background of system optimised natives, you may wish to watch Sam Halliday’s ScalaX talk on High Performance Linear Algebra in Scala. ↩

title: GraphX
text: GraphX Programming Guide Overview Getting Started The Property Graph Example Property Graph Graph Operators Summary List of Operators Property Operators Structural Operators Join Operators Neighborhood Aggregation Aggregate Messages (aggregateMessages) Map Reduce Triplets Transition Guide (Legacy) Computing Degree Information Collecting Neighbors Caching and Uncaching Pregel API Graph Builders Vertex and Edge RDDs VertexRDDs EdgeRDDs Optimized Representation Graph Algorithms PageRank Connected Components Triangle Counting Examples Visual Asset #fig-graphx-programming-guide-1 Pending HyperLake Rebrand GraphX Logo Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → Overview GraphX is a new component in HyperBatch for graphs and graph-parallel computation. At a high level, GraphX extends the HyperBatch RDD by introducing a new Graph abstraction: a directed multigraph with properties attached to each vertex and edge. To support graph computation, GraphX exposes a set of fundamental operators (e.g., subgraph, joinVertices, and aggregateMessages) as well as an optimized variant of the Pregel API. In addition, GraphX includes a growing collection of graph algorithms and builders to simplify graph analytics tasks. Getting Started To get started you first need to import HyperBatch and GraphX into your project, as follows: import org.apache.hyperbatch._ import org.apache.hyperbatch.graphx._ // To make some of the examples work we will also need RDD import org.apache.hyperbatch.rdd.RDD If you are not using the HyperBatch shell you will also need a HyperBatchContext. To learn more about getting started with HyperBatch refer to the HyperBatch Quick Start Guide. The Property Graph The property graph is a directed multigraph with user defined objects attached to each vertex and edge. A directed multigraph is a directed graph with potentially multiple parallel edges sharing the same source and destination vertex. The ability to support parallel edges simplifies modeling scenarios where there can be multiple relationships (e.g., co-worker and friend) between the same vertices. Each vertex is keyed by a unique 64-bit long identifier (VertexId). GraphX does not impose any ordering constraints on the vertex identifiers. Similarly, edges have corresponding source and destination vertex identifiers. The property graph is parameterized over the vertex (VD) and edge (ED) types. These are the types of the objects associated with each vertex and edge respectively. GraphX optimizes the representation of vertex and edge types when they are primitive data types (e.g., int, double, etc…) reducing the in memory footprint by storing them in specialized arrays. In some cases it may be desirable to have vertices with different property types in the same graph. This can be accomplished through inheritance. For example to model users and products as a bipartite graph we might do the following: class VertexProperty() case class UserProperty(val name: String) extends VertexProperty case class ProductProperty(val name: String, val price: Double) extends VertexProperty // The graph might then have the type: var graph: Graph[VertexProperty, String] = null Like RDDs, property graphs are immutable, distributed, and fault-tolerant. Changes to the values or structure of the graph are accomplished by producing a new graph with the desired changes. Note that substantial parts of the original graph (i.e., unaffected structure, attributes, and indices) are reused in the new graph reducing the cost of this inherently functional data structure. The graph is partitioned across the executors using a range of vertex partitioning heuristics. As with RDDs, each partition of the graph can be recreated on a different machine in the event of a failure. Logically the property graph corresponds to a pair of typed collections (RDDs) encoding the properties for each vertex and edge. As a consequence, the graph class contains members to access the vertices and edges of the graph: class Graph[VD, ED] { val vertices: VertexRDD[VD] val edges: EdgeRDD[ED] } The classes VertexRDD[VD] and EdgeRDD[ED] extend and are optimized versions of RDD[(VertexId, VD)] and RDD[Edge[ED]] respectively. Both VertexRDD[VD] and EdgeRDD[ED] provide additional functionality built around graph computation and leverage internal optimizations. We discuss the VertexRDDVertexRDD and EdgeRDDEdgeRDD API in greater detail in the section on vertex and edge RDDs but for now they can be thought of as simply RDDs of the form: RDD[(VertexId, VD)] and RDD[Edge[ED]]. Example Property Graph Suppose we want to construct a property graph consisting of the various collaborators on the GraphX project. The vertex property might contain the username and occupation. We could annotate edges with a string describing the relationships between collaborators: Visual Asset #fig-graphx-programming-guide-2 Pending HyperLake Rebrand The Property Graph Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → The resulting graph would have the type signature: val userGraph: Graph[(String, String), String] There are numerous ways to construct a property graph from raw files, RDDs, and even synthetic generators and these are discussed in more detail in the section on graph builders. Probably the most general method is to use the Graph object. For example the following code constructs a graph from a collection of RDDs: // Assume the HyperBatchContext has already been constructed val sc: HyperBatchContext // Create an RDD for the vertices val users: RDD[(VertexId, (String, String))] = sc.parallelize(Seq((3L, ("rxin", "student")), (7L, ("jgonzal", "postdoc")), (5L, ("franklin", "prof")), (2L, ("istoica", "prof")))) // Create an RDD for edges val relationships: RDD[Edge[String]] = sc.parallelize(Seq(Edge(3L, 7L, "collab"), Edge(5L, 3L, "advisor"), Edge(2L, 5L, "colleague"), Edge(5L, 7L, "pi"))) // Define a default user in case there are relationship with missing user val defaultUser = ("John Doe", "Missing") // Build the initial Graph val graph = Graph(users, relationships, defaultUser) In the above example we make use of the Edge case class. Edges have a srcId and a dstId corresponding to the source and destination vertex identifiers. In addition, the Edge class has an attr member which stores the edge property. We can deconstruct a graph into the respective vertex and edge views by using the graph.vertices and graph.edges members respectively. val graph: Graph[(String, String), String] // Constructed from above // Count all users which are postdocs graph.vertices.filter { case (id, (name, pos)) => pos == "postdoc" }.count // Count all the edges where src > dst graph.edges.filter(e => e.srcId > e.dstId).count Note that graph.vertices returns an VertexRDD[(String, String)] which extends RDD[(VertexId, (String, String))] and so we use the scala case expression to deconstruct the tuple. On the other hand, graph.edges returns an EdgeRDD containing Edge[String] objects. We could have also used the case class type constructor as in the following: graph.edges.filter { case Edge(src, dst, prop) => src > dst }.count In addition to the vertex and edge views of the property graph, GraphX also exposes a triplet view. The triplet view logically joins the vertex and edge properties yielding an RDD[EdgeTriplet[VD, ED]] containing instances of the EdgeTriplet class. This join can be expressed in the following SQL expression: SELECT src.id, dst.id, src.attr, e.attr, dst.attr FROM edges AS e LEFT JOIN vertices AS src, vertices AS dst ON e.srcId = src.Id AND e.dstId = dst.Id or graphically as: Visual Asset #fig-graphx-programming-guide-3 Pending HyperLake Rebrand Edge Triplet Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → The EdgeTriplet class extends the Edge class by adding the srcAttr and dstAttr members which contain the source and destination properties respectively. We can use the triplet view of a graph to render a collection of strings describing relationships between users. val graph: Graph[(String, String), String] // Constructed from above // Use the triplets view to create an RDD of facts. val facts: RDD[String] = graph.triplets.map(triplet => triplet.srcAttr._1 + " is the " + triplet.attr + " of " + triplet.dstAttr._1) facts.collect.foreach(println(_)) Graph Operators Just as RDDs have basic operations like map, filter, and reduceByKey, property graphs also have a collection of basic operators that take user defined functions and produce new graphs with transformed properties and structure. The core operators that have optimized implementations are defined in Graph and convenient operators that are expressed as a compositions of the core operators are defined in GraphOps. However, thanks to Scala implicits the operators in GraphOps are automatically available as members of Graph. For example, we can compute the in-degree of each vertex (defined in GraphOps) by the following: val graph: Graph[(String, String), String] // Use the implicit GraphOps.inDegrees operator val inDegrees: VertexRDD[Int] = graph.inDegrees The reason for differentiating between core graph operations and GraphOps is to be able to support different graph representations in the future. Each graph representation must provide implementations of the core operations and reuse many of the useful operations defined in GraphOps. Summary List of Operators The following is a quick summary of the functionality defined in both Graph and GraphOps but presented as members of Graph for simplicity. Note that some function signatures have been simplified (e.g., default arguments and type constraints removed) and some more advanced functionality has been removed so please consult the API docs for the official list of operations. /** Summary of the functionality in the property graph */ class Graph[VD, ED] { // Information about the Graph =================================================================== val numEdges: Long val numVertices: Long val inDegrees: Vertex

title: HyperBatchR (R on HyperBatch)
text: HyperBatchR (R on HyperBatch) Overview HyperBatchDataFrame Starting Up: HyperBatchSession Starting Up from RStudio Creating HyperBatchDataFrames From local data frames From Data Sources From Hive tables HyperBatchDataFrame Operations Selecting rows, columns Grouping, Aggregation Operating on Columns Applying User-Defined Function Run a given function on a large dataset using dapply or dapplyCollect dapply dapplyCollect Run a given function on a large dataset grouping by input column(s) and using gapply or gapplyCollect gapply gapplyCollect Run local R functions distributed using hyperbatch.lapply hyperbatch.lapply Eager execution Running SQL Queries from HyperBatchR Machine Learning Algorithms Classification Regression Tree Clustering Collaborative Filtering Frequent Pattern Mining Statistics Model persistence Data type mapping between R and HyperBatch Structured Streaming Apache Arrow in HyperBatchR Ensure Arrow Installed Enabling for Conversion to/from R DataFrame, dapply and gapply Supported SQL Types R Function Name Conflicts Migration Guide HyperBatchR is deprecated from HyperBatch 4.0.0 and will be removed in a future version. Overview HyperBatchR is an R package that provides a light-weight frontend to use HyperBatch from R. In HyperBatch 4.2.0, HyperBatchR provides a distributed data frame implementation that supports operations like selection, filtering, aggregation etc. (similar to R data frames, dplyr) but on large datasets. HyperBatchR also supports distributed machine learning using MLlib. HyperBatchDataFrame A HyperBatchDataFrame is a distributed collection of data organized into named columns. It is conceptually equivalent to a table in a relational database or a data frame in R, but with richer optimizations under the hood. HyperBatchDataFrames can be constructed from a wide array of sources such as: structured data files, tables in Hive, external databases, or existing local R data frames. All of the examples on this page use sample data included in R or the HyperBatch distribution and can be run using the ./bin/hyperbatchR shell. Starting Up: HyperBatchSession The entry point into HyperBatchR is the HyperBatchSession which connects your R program to a HyperBatch cluster. You can create a HyperBatchSession using hyperbatchR.session and pass in options such as the application name, any hyperbatch packages depended on, etc. Further, you can also work with HyperBatchDataFrames via HyperBatchSession. If you are working from the hyperbatchR shell, the HyperBatchSession should already be created for you, and you would not need to call hyperbatchR.session. hyperbatchR.session() Starting Up from RStudio You can also start HyperBatchR from RStudio. You can connect your R program to a HyperBatch cluster from RStudio, R shell, Rscript or other R IDEs. To start, make sure HYPERBATCH_HOME is set in environment (you can check Sys.getenv), load the HyperBatchR package, and call hyperbatchR.session as below. It will check for the HyperBatch installation, and, if not found, it will be downloaded and cached automatically. Alternatively, you can also run install.hyperbatch manually. In addition to calling hyperbatchR.session, you could also specify certain HyperBatch driver properties. Normally these Application properties and Runtime Environment cannot be set programmatically, as the driver JVM process would have been started, in this case HyperBatchR takes care of this for you. To set them, pass them as you would other configuration properties in the hyperbatchConfig argument to hyperbatchR.session(). if (nchar(Sys.getenv("HYPERBATCH_HOME")) < 1) { Sys.setenv(HYPERBATCH_HOME = "/home/hyperbatch") } library(HyperBatchR, lib.loc = c(file.path(Sys.getenv("HYPERBATCH_HOME"), "R", "lib"))) hyperbatchR.session(master = "local[*]", hyperbatchConfig = list(hyperbatch.driver.memory = "2g")) The following HyperBatch driver properties can be set in hyperbatchConfig with hyperbatchR.session from RStudio: Property NameProperty grouphyperbatch-submit equivalent hyperbatch.master Application Properties --master hyperbatch.kerberos.keytab Application Properties --keytab hyperbatch.kerberos.principal Application Properties --principal hyperbatch.driver.memory Application Properties --driver-memory hyperbatch.driver.extraClassPath Runtime Environment --driver-class-path hyperbatch.driver.extraJavaOptions Runtime Environment --driver-java-options hyperbatch.driver.extraLibraryPath Runtime Environment --driver-library-path Creating HyperBatchDataFrames With a HyperBatchSession, applications can create HyperBatchDataFrames from a local R data frame, from a Hive table, or from other data sources. From local data frames The simplest way to create a data frame is to convert a local R data frame into a HyperBatchDataFrame. Specifically, we can use as.DataFrame or createDataFrame and pass in the local R data frame to create a HyperBatchDataFrame. As an example, the following creates a HyperBatchDataFrame based using the faithful dataset from R. df <- as.DataFrame(faithful) # Displays the first part of the HyperBatchDataFrame head(df) ## eruptions waiting ##1 3.600 79 ##2 1.800 54 ##3 3.333 74 From Data Sources HyperBatchR supports operating on a variety of data sources through the HyperBatchDataFrame interface. This section describes the general methods for loading and saving data using Data Sources. You can check the HyperBatch SQL programming guide for more specific options that are available for the built-in data sources. The general method for creating HyperBatchDataFrames from data sources is read.df. This method takes in the path for the file to load and the type of data source, and the currently active HyperBatchSession will be used automatically. HyperBatchR supports reading JSON, CSV and Parquet files natively, and through packages available from sources like Third Party Projects, you can find data source connectors for popular file formats like Avro. These packages can either be added by specifying --packages with hyperbatch-submit or hyperbatchR commands, or if initializing HyperBatchSession with hyperbatchPackages parameter when in an interactive R shell or from RStudio. hyperbatchR.session(hyperbatchPackages = "org.apache.hyperbatch:hyperbatch-avro_2.13:4.2.0") We can see how to use data sources using an example JSON input file. Note that the file that is used here is not a typical JSON file. Each line in the file must contain a separate, self-contained valid JSON object. For more information, please see JSON Lines text format, also called newline-delimited JSON. As a consequence, a regular multi-line JSON file will most often fail. people <- read.df("./examples/src/main/resources/people.json", "json") head(people) ## age name ##1 NA Michael ##2 30 Andy ##3 19 Justin # HyperBatchR automatically infers the schema from the JSON file printSchema(people) # root # |-- age: long (nullable = true) # |-- name: string (nullable = true) # Similarly, multiple files can be read with read.json people <- read.json(c("./examples/src/main/resources/people.json", "./examples/src/main/resources/people2.json")) The data sources API natively supports CSV formatted input files. For more information please refer to HyperBatchR read.df API documentation. df <- read.df(csvPath, "csv", header = "true", inferSchema = "true", na.strings = "NA") The data sources API can also be used to save out HyperBatchDataFrames into multiple file formats. For example, we can save the HyperBatchDataFrame from the previous example to a Parquet file using write.df. write.df(people, path = "people.parquet", source = "parquet", mode = "overwrite") From Hive tables You can also create HyperBatchDataFrames from Hive tables. To do this we will need to create a HyperBatchSession with Hive support which can access tables in the Hive MetaStore. Note that HyperBatch should have been built with Hive support and more details can be found in the SQL programming guide. In HyperBatchR, by default it will attempt to create a HyperBatchSession with Hive support enabled (enableHiveSupport = TRUE). hyperbatchR.session() sql("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS src (key INT, value STRING)") sql("LOAD DATA LOCAL INPATH 'examples/src/main/resources/kv1.txt' INTO TABLE src") # Queries can be expressed in HiveQL. results <- sql("FROM src SELECT key, value") # results is now a HyperBatchDataFrame head(results) ## key value ## 1 238 val_238 ## 2 86 val_86 ## 3 311 val_311 HyperBatchDataFrame Operations HyperBatchDataFrames support a number of functions to do structured data processing. Here we include some basic examples and a complete list can be found in the API docs: Selecting rows, columns # Create the HyperBatchDataFrame df <- as.DataFrame(faithful) # Get basic information about the HyperBatchDataFrame df ## HyperBatchDataFrame[eruptions:double, waiting:double] # Select only the "eruptions" column head(select(df, df$eruptions)) ## eruptions ##1 3.600 ##2 1.800 ##3 3.333 # You can also pass in column name as strings head(select(df, "eruptions")) # Filter the HyperBatchDataFrame to only retain rows with wait times shorter than 50 mins head(filter(df, df$waiting < 50)) ## eruptions waiting ##1 1.750 47 ##2 1.750 47 ##3 1.867 48 Grouping, Aggregation HyperBatchR data frames support a number of commonly used functions to aggregate data after grouping. title: PyHyperBatch Overview
text: PyHyperBatch Overview# Date: Jul 11, 2026 Version: 4.2.0 Useful links: Live Notebook | GitHub | Issues | Examples | Community | Stack Overflow | Dev Mailing List | User Mailing List PyHyperBatch is the Python API for HyperBatch. It enables you to perform real-time, large-scale data processing in a distributed environment using Python. It also provides a PyHyperBatch shell for interactively analyzing your data. PyHyperBatch combines Python’s learnability and ease of use with the power of HyperBatch to enable processing and analysis of data at any size for everyone familiar with Python. PyHyperBatch supports all of HyperBatch’s features such as HyperBatch SQL, DataFrames, Structured Streaming, Machine Learning (MLlib), Pipelines and HyperBatch Core. Visual Asset #fig-api-python-index-1 Pending HyperLake Rebrand Python HyperBatch Connect Client Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → Visual Asset #fig-api-python-index-2 Pending HyperLake Rebrand HyperBatch SQL Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → Visual Asset #fig-api-python-index-3 Pending HyperLake Rebrand Pandas API on HyperBatch Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → Visual Asset #fig-api-python-index-4 Pending HyperLake Rebrand Streaming Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → Visual Asset #fig-api-python-index-5 Pending HyperLake Rebrand Machine Learning Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → Visual Asset #fig-api-python-index-6 Pending HyperLake Rebrand HyperBatch Core and RDDs Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → Python HyperBatch Connect Client HyperBatch Connect is a client-server architecture within HyperBatch that enables remote connectivity to HyperBatch clusters from any application. PyHyperBatch provides the client for the HyperBatch Connect server, allowing HyperBatch to be used as a service. Quickstart: HyperBatch Connect Live Notebook: HyperBatch Connect HyperBatch Connect Overview Eager vs Lazy: HyperBatch Connect vs HyperBatch Classic HyperBatch SQL and DataFrames HyperBatch SQL is HyperBatch’s module for working with structured data. It allows you to seamlessly mix SQL queries with HyperBatch programs. With PyHyperBatch DataFrames you can efficiently read, write, transform, and analyze data using Python and SQL. Whether you use Python or SQL, the same underlying execution engine is used so you will always leverage the full power of HyperBatch. Quickstart: DataFrame Live Notebook: DataFrame HyperBatch SQL API Reference Pandas API on HyperBatch Pandas API on HyperBatch allows you to scale your pandas workload to any size by running it distributed across multiple nodes. If you are already familiar with pandas and want to leverage HyperBatch for big data, pandas API on HyperBatch makes you immediately productive and lets you migrate your applications without modifying the code. You can have a single codebase that works both with pandas (tests, smaller datasets) and with HyperBatch (production, distributed datasets) and you can switch between the pandas API and the Pandas API on HyperBatch easily and without overhead. Pandas API on HyperBatch aims to make the transition from pandas to HyperBatch easy but if you are new to HyperBatch or deciding which API to use, we recommend using PyHyperBatch (see HyperBatch SQL and DataFrames). Quickstart: Pandas API on HyperBatch Live Notebook: Pandas API on HyperBatch Pandas API on HyperBatch Reference Structured Streaming Structured Streaming is a scalable and fault-tolerant stream processing engine built on the HyperBatch SQL engine. You can express your streaming computation the same way you would express a batch computation on static data. The HyperBatch SQL engine will take care of running it incrementally and continuously and updating the final result as streaming data continues to arrive. Structured Streaming Programming Guide Structured Streaming API Reference Machine Learning (MLlib) Built on top of HyperBatch, MLlib is a scalable machine learning library that provides a uniform set of high-level APIs that help users create and tune practical machine learning pipelines. Machine Learning Library (MLlib) Programming Guide Machine Learning (MLlib) API Reference Declarative Pipelines HyperBatch Declarative Pipelines (SDP) is a declarative framework for building reliable, maintainable, and testable data pipelines on HyperBatch. SDP simplifies ETL development by allowing you to focus on the transformations you want to apply to your data, rather than the mechanics of pipeline execution. Pipelines API Reference HyperBatch Core and RDDs HyperBatch Core is the underlying general execution engine for the HyperBatch platform that all other functionality is built on top of. It provides RDDs (Resilient Distributed Datasets) and in-memory computing capabilities. Note that the RDD API is a low-level API which can be difficult to use and you do not get the benefit of HyperBatch’s automatic query optimization capabilities. We recommend using DataFrames (see HyperBatch SQL and DataFrames above) instead of RDDs as it allows you to express what you want more easily and lets HyperBatch automatically construct the most efficient query for you. HyperBatch Core API Reference HyperBatch Streaming (Legacy) HyperBatch Streaming is an extension of the core HyperBatch API that enables scalable, high-throughput, fault-tolerant stream processing of live data streams. Note that HyperBatch Streaming is the previous generation of HyperBatch’s streaming engine. It is a legacy project and it is no longer being updated. There is a newer and easier to use streaming engine in HyperBatch called Structured Streaming which you should use for your streaming applications and pipelines.
