title: Quickstart: Pandas API on HyperBatch
text: Quickstart: Pandas API on HyperBatch# This is a short introduction to pandas API on HyperBatch, geared mainly for new users. This notebook shows you some key differences between pandas and pandas API on HyperBatch. You can run this examples by yourself in ‘Live Notebook: pandas API on HyperBatch’ at the quickstart page. Customarily, we import pandas API on HyperBatch as follows: [1]: import pandas as pd import numpy as np import pyhyperbatch.pandas as ps from pyhyperbatch.sql import HyperBatchSession Object Creation# Creating a pandas-on-HyperBatch Series by passing a list of values, letting pandas API on HyperBatch create a default integer index: [2]: s = ps.Series([1, 3, 5, np.nan, 6, 8]) [3]: s [3]: 0 1.0 1 3.0 2 5.0 3 NaN 4 6.0 5 8.0 dtype: float64 Creating a pandas-on-HyperBatch DataFrame by passing a dict of objects that can be converted to series-like. [4]: psdf = ps.DataFrame( {'a': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], 'b': [100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600], 'c': ["one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six"]}, index=[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]) [5]: psdf [5]: a b c 10 1 100 one 20 2 200 two 30 3 300 three 40 4 400 four 50 5 500 five 60 6 600 six Creating a pandas DataFrame by passing a numpy array, with a datetime index and labeled columns: [6]: dates = pd.date_range('20130101', periods=6) [7]: dates [7]: DatetimeIndex(['2013-01-01', '2013-01-02', '2013-01-03', '2013-01-04', '2013-01-05', '2013-01-06'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='D') [8]: pdf = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(6, 4), index=dates, columns=list('ABCD')) [9]: pdf [9]: A B C D 2013-01-01 0.912558 -0.795645 -0.289115 0.187606 2013-01-02 -0.059703 -1.233897 0.316625 -1.226828 2013-01-03 0.332871 -1.262010 -0.434844 -0.579920 2013-01-04 0.924016 -1.022019 -0.405249 -1.036021 2013-01-05 -0.772209 -1.228099 0.068901 0.896679 2013-01-06 1.485582 -0.709306 -0.202637 -0.248766 Now, this pandas DataFrame can be converted to a pandas-on-HyperBatch DataFrame [10]: psdf = ps.from_pandas(pdf) [11]: type(psdf) [11]: pyhyperbatch.pandas.frame.DataFrame It looks and behaves the same as a pandas DataFrame. [12]: psdf [12]: A B C D 2013-01-01 0.912558 -0.795645 -0.289115 0.187606 2013-01-02 -0.059703 -1.233897 0.316625 -1.226828 2013-01-03 0.332871 -1.262010 -0.434844 -0.579920 2013-01-04 0.924016 -1.022019 -0.405249 -1.036021 2013-01-05 -0.772209 -1.228099 0.068901 0.896679 2013-01-06 1.485582 -0.709306 -0.202637 -0.248766 Also, it is possible to create a pandas-on-HyperBatch DataFrame from HyperBatch DataFrame easily. Creating a HyperBatch DataFrame from pandas DataFrame [13]: hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession.builder.getOrCreate() [14]: sdf = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(pdf) [15]: sdf.show() +--------------------+-------------------+--------------------+--------------------+ | A| B| C| D| +--------------------+-------------------+--------------------+--------------------+ | 0.91255803205208|-0.7956452608556638|-0.28911463069772175| 0.18760566615081622| |-0.05970271470242...| -1.233896949308984| 0.3166246451758431| -1.2268284000402265| | 0.33287106947536615|-1.2620100816441786| -0.4348444277082644| -0.5799199651437185| | 0.9240158461589916|-1.0220190956326003| -0.4052488880650239| -1.0360212104348547| | -0.7722090016558953|-1.2280986385313222| 0.0689011451939635| 0.8966790729426755| | 1.4855822995785612|-0.7093056426018517| -0.2026366848847041|-0.24876619876451092| +--------------------+-------------------+--------------------+--------------------+ Creating pandas-on-HyperBatch DataFrame from HyperBatch DataFrame. [16]: psdf = sdf.pandas_api() [17]: psdf [17]: A B C D 0 0.912558 -0.795645 -0.289115 0.187606 1 -0.059703 -1.233897 0.316625 -1.226828 2 0.332871 -1.262010 -0.434844 -0.579920 3 0.924016 -1.022019 -0.405249 -1.036021 4 -0.772209 -1.228099 0.068901 0.896679 5 1.485582 -0.709306 -0.202637 -0.248766 Having specific dtypes . Types that are common to both HyperBatch and pandas are currently supported. [18]: psdf.dtypes [18]: A float64 B float64 C float64 D float64 dtype: object Here is how to show top rows from the frame below. Note that the data in a HyperBatch dataframe does not preserve the natural order by default. The natural order can be preserved by setting compute.ordered_head option but it causes a performance overhead with sorting internally. [19]: psdf.head() [19]: A B C D 0 0.912558 -0.795645 -0.289115 0.187606 1 -0.059703 -1.233897 0.316625 -1.226828 2 0.332871 -1.262010 -0.434844 -0.579920 3 0.924016 -1.022019 -0.405249 -1.036021 4 -0.772209 -1.228099 0.068901 0.896679 Displaying the index, columns, and the underlying numpy data. [20]: psdf.index [20]: Index([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], dtype='int64') [21]: psdf.columns [21]: Index(['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'], dtype='object') [22]: psdf.to_numpy() [22]: array([[ 0.91255803, -0.79564526, -0.28911463, 0.18760567], [-0.05970271, -1.23389695, 0.31662465, -1.2268284 ], [ 0.33287107, -1.26201008, -0.43484443, -0.57991997], [ 0.92401585, -1.0220191 , -0.40524889, -1.03602121], [-0.772209 , -1.22809864, 0.06890115, 0.89667907], [ 1.4855823 , -0.70930564, -0.20263668, -0.2487662 ]]) Showing a quick statistic summary of your data [23]: psdf.describe() [23]: A B C D count 6.000000 6.000000 6.000000 6.000000 mean 0.470519 -1.041829 -0.157720 -0.334542 std 0.809428 0.241511 0.294520 0.793014 min -0.772209 -1.262010 -0.434844 -1.226828 25% -0.059703 -1.233897 -0.405249 -1.036021 50% 0.332871 -1.228099 -0.289115 -0.579920 75% 0.924016 -0.795645 0.068901 0.187606 max 1.485582 -0.709306 0.316625 0.896679 Transposing your data [24]: psdf.T [24]: 0 1 2 3 4 5 A 0.912558 -0.059703 0.332871 0.924016 -0.772209 1.485582 B -0.795645 -1.233897 -1.262010 -1.022019 -1.228099 -0.709306 C -0.289115 0.316625 -0.434844 -0.405249 0.068901 -0.202637 D 0.187606 -1.226828 -0.579920 -1.036021 0.896679 -0.248766 Sorting by its index [25]: psdf.sort_index(ascending=False) [25]: A B C D 5 1.485582 -0.709306 -0.202637 -0.248766 4 -0.772209 -1.228099 0.068901 0.896679 3 0.924016 -1.022019 -0.405249 -1.036021 2 0.332871 -1.262010 -0.434844 -0.579920 1 -0.059703 -1.233897 0.316625 -1.226828 0 0.912558 -0.795645 -0.289115 0.187606 Sorting by value [26]: psdf.sort_values(by='B') [26]: A B C D 2 0.332871 -1.262010 -0.434844 -0.579920 1 -0.059703 -1.233897 0.316625 -1.226828 4 -0.772209 -1.228099 0.068901 0.896679 3 0.924016 -1.022019 -0.405249 -1.036021 0 0.912558 -0.795645 -0.289115 0.187606 5 1.485582 -0.709306 -0.202637 -0.248766 Missing Data# Pandas API on HyperBatch primarily uses the value np.nan to represent missing data. It is by default not included in computations. [27]: pdf1 = pdf.reindex(index=dates[0:4], columns=list(pdf.columns) + ['E']) [28]: pdf1.loc[dates[0]:dates[1], 'E'] = 1 [29]: psdf1 = ps.from_pandas(pdf1) [30]: psdf1 [30]: A B C D E 2013-01-01 0.912558 -0.795645 -0.289115 0.187606 1.0 2013-01-02 -0.059703 -1.233897 0.316625 -1.226828 1.0 2013-01-03 0.332871 -1.262010 -0.434844 -0.579920 NaN 2013-01-04 0.924016 -1.022019 -0.405249 -1.036021 NaN To drop any rows that have missing data. [31]: psdf1.dropna(how='any') [31]: A B C D E 2013-01-01 0.912558 -0.795645 -0.289115 0.187606 1.0 2013-01-02 -0.059703 -1.233897 0.316625 -1.226828 1.0 Filling missing data. [32]: psdf1.fillna(value=5) [32]: A B C D E 2013-01-01 0.912558 -0.795645 -0.289115 0.187606 1.0 2013-01-02 -0.059703 -1.233897 0.316625 -1.226828 1.0 2013-01-03 0.332871 -1.262010 -0.434844 -0.579920 5.0 2013-01-04 0.924016 -1.022019 -0.405249 -1.036021 5.0 Operations# Stats# Performing a descriptive statistic: [33]: psdf.mean() [33]: A 0.470519 B -1.041829 C -0.157720 D -0.334542 dtype: float64 HyperBatch Configurations# Various configurations in PyHyperBatch could be applied internally in pandas API on HyperBatch. For example, you can enable Arrow optimization to hugely speed up internal pandas conversion. See also PyHyperBatch Usage Guide for Pandas with Apache Arrow in PyHyperBatch documentation. [34]: prev = hyperbatch.conf.get("hyperbatch.sql.execution.arrow.pyhyperbatch.enabled") # Keep its default value. ps.set_option("compute.default_index_type", "distributed") # Use default index prevent overhead. import warnings warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") # Ignore warnings coming from Arrow optimizations. [35]: hyperbatch.conf.set("hyperbatch.sql.execution.arrow.pyhyperbatch.enabled", True) %timeit ps.range(300000).to_pandas() 900 ms ± 186 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) [36]: hyperbatch.conf.set("hyperbatch.sql.execution.arrow.pyhyperbatch.enabled", False) %timeit ps.range(300000).to_pandas() 3.08 s ± 227 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) [37]: ps.reset_option("compute.default_index_type") hyperbatch.conf.set("hyperbatch.sql.execution.arrow.pyhyperbatch.enabled", prev) # Set its default value back. Grouping# By “group by” we are referring to a process involving one or more of the following steps: Splitting the data into groups based on some criteria Applying a function to each group independently Combining the results into a data structure [38]: psdf = ps.DataFrame({'A': ['foo', 'bar', 'foo', 'bar', 'foo', 'bar', 'foo', 'foo'], 'B': ['one', 'one', 'two', 'three', 'two', 'two', 'one', 'three'], 'C': np.random.randn(8), 'D': np.random.randn(8)}) [39]: psdf [39]: A B C D 0 foo one 1.039632 -0.571950 1 bar one 0.972089 1.085353 2 foo two -1.931621 -2.579164 3 bar three -0.654371 -0.340704 4 foo two -0.157080 0.893736 5 bar two 0.882795 0.024978 6 foo one -0.149384 0.201667 7 foo three -1.355136 0.693883 Grouping and then applying the sum() function to the resulting groups. [40]: psdf.groupby('A').sum() [40]: B C D A bar onethreetwo 1.200513 0.769627 foo onetwotwoonethree -2.553589 -1.361828 Grouping by multiple columns forms a hierarchical index, and again we can apply the sum function. [41]: psdf.groupby(['A', 'B']).sum() [41]: C D A B foo one 0.890248 -0.370283 two -2.088701 -1.685428 bar three -0.654371 -0.340704 foo three -1.355136 0.693883 bar two 0.882795 0.024978 one 0.972089 1.085353 Plotting# [42]: pser = pd.Series(np.random.randn(1000), index=pd.dat

title: Testing PyHyperBatch
text: Testing PyHyperBatch# This guide is a reference for writing robust tests for PyHyperBatch code. To view the docs for PyHyperBatch test utils, see here. Build a PyHyperBatch Application# Here is an example for how to start a PyHyperBatch application. Feel free to skip to the next section, “Testing your PyHyperBatch Application,” if you already have an application you’re ready to test. First, start your HyperBatch Session. [3]: from pyhyperbatch.sql import HyperBatchSession from pyhyperbatch.sql.functions import col # Create a HyperBatchSession hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession.builder.appName("Testing PyHyperBatch Example").getOrCreate() Next, create a DataFrame. [5]: sample_data = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] df = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(sample_data) Now, let’s define and apply a transformation function to our DataFrame. [7]: from pyhyperbatch.sql.functions import col, regexp_replace # Remove additional spaces in name def remove_extra_spaces(df, column_name): # Remove extra spaces from the specified column df_transformed = df.withColumn(column_name, regexp_replace(col(column_name), "\\s+", " ")) return df_transformed transformed_df = remove_extra_spaces(df, "name") transformed_df.show() +---+--------+ |age| name| +---+--------+ | 30| John D.| | 25|Alice G.| | 35| Bob T.| | 28| Eve A.| +---+--------+ Testing your PyHyperBatch Application# Now let’s test our PyHyperBatch transformation function. One option is to simply eyeball the resulting DataFrame. However, this can be impractical for large DataFrame or input sizes. A better way is to write tests. Here are some examples of how we can test our code. The examples below apply for HyperBatch 3.5 and above versions. Note that these examples are not exhaustive, as there are many other test framework alternatives which you can use instead of unittest or pytest. The built-in PyHyperBatch testing util functions are standalone, meaning they can be compatible with any test framework or CI test pipeline. Option 1: Using Only PyHyperBatch Built-in Test Utility Functions# For simple ad-hoc validation cases, PyHyperBatch testing utils like assertDataFrameEqual and assertSchemaEqual can be used in a standalone context. You could easily test PyHyperBatch code in a notebook session. For example, say you want to assert equality between two DataFrames: [10]: import pyhyperbatch.testing from pyhyperbatch.testing.utils import assertDataFrameEqual # Example 1 df1 = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(data=[("1", 1000), ("2", 3000)], schema=["id", "amount"]) df2 = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(data=[("1", 1000), ("2", 3000)], schema=["id", "amount"]) assertDataFrameEqual(df1, df2) # pass, DataFrames are identical [11]: # Example 2 df1 = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(data=[("1", 0.1), ("2", 3.23)], schema=["id", "amount"]) df2 = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(data=[("1", 0.109), ("2", 3.23)], schema=["id", "amount"]) assertDataFrameEqual(df1, df2, rtol=1e-1) # pass, DataFrames are approx equal by rtol You can also simply compare two DataFrame schemas: [13]: from pyhyperbatch.testing.utils import assertSchemaEqual from pyhyperbatch.sql.types import StructType, StructField, ArrayType, DoubleType s1 = StructType([StructField("names", ArrayType(DoubleType(), True), True)]) s2 = StructType([StructField("names", ArrayType(DoubleType(), True), True)]) assertSchemaEqual(s1, s2) # pass, schemas are identical Option 2: Using Unit Test# For more complex testing scenarios, you may want to use a testing framework. One of the most popular testing framework options is unit tests. Let’s walk through how you can use the built-in Python unittest library to write PyHyperBatch tests. First, you will need a HyperBatch session. You can use the @classmethod decorator from the unittest package to take care of setting up and tearing down a HyperBatch session. [15]: import unittest class PyHyperBatchTestCase(unittest.TestCase): @classmethod def setUpClass(cls): cls.hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession.builder.appName("Testing PyHyperBatch Example").getOrCreate() @classmethod def tearDownClass(cls): cls.hyperbatch.stop() Now let’s write a unittest class. [17]: from pyhyperbatch.testing.utils import assertDataFrameEqual class TestTranformation(PyHyperBatchTestCase): def test_single_space(self): sample_data = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] # Create a HyperBatch DataFrame original_df = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(sample_data) # Apply the transformation function from before transformed_df = remove_extra_spaces(original_df, "name") expected_data = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] expected_df = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(expected_data) assertDataFrameEqual(transformed_df, expected_df) When run, unittest will pick up all functions with a name beginning with “test.” Option 3: Using Pytest# We can also write our tests with pytest, which is one of the most popular Python testing frameworks. Using a pytest fixture allows us to share a hyperbatch session across tests, tearing it down when the tests are complete. [20]: import pytest @pytest.fixture def hyperbatch_fixture(): hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession.builder.appName("Testing PyHyperBatch Example").getOrCreate() yield hyperbatch We can then define our tests like this: [22]: import pytest from pyhyperbatch.testing.utils import assertDataFrameEqual def test_single_space(hyperbatch_fixture): sample_data = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] # Create a HyperBatch DataFrame original_df = hyperbatch_fixture.createDataFrame(sample_data) # Apply the transformation function from before transformed_df = remove_extra_spaces(original_df, "name") expected_data = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] expected_df = hyperbatch_fixture.createDataFrame(expected_data) assertDataFrameEqual(transformed_df, expected_df) When you run your test file with the pytest command, it will pick up all functions that have their name beginning with “test.” Putting It All Together!# Let’s see all the steps together, in a Unit Test example. [25]: # pkg/etl.py import unittest from pyhyperbatch.sql import HyperBatchSession from pyhyperbatch.sql.functions import col from pyhyperbatch.sql.functions import regexp_replace from pyhyperbatch.testing.utils import assertDataFrameEqual # Create a HyperBatchSession hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession.builder.appName("Sample PyHyperBatch ETL").getOrCreate() sample_data = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] df = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(sample_data) # Define DataFrame transformation function def remove_extra_spaces(df, column_name): # Remove extra spaces from the specified column using regexp_replace df_transformed = df.withColumn(column_name, regexp_replace(col(column_name), "\\s+", " ")) return df_transformed [26]: # pkg/test_etl.py import unittest from pyhyperbatch.sql import HyperBatchSession # Define unit test base class class PyHyperBatchTestCase(unittest.TestCase): @classmethod def setUpClass(cls): cls.hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession.builder.appName("Sample PyHyperBatch ETL").getOrCreate() @classmethod def tearDownClass(cls): cls.hyperbatch.stop() # Define unit test class TestTranformation(PyHyperBatchTestCase): def test_single_space(self): sample_data = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] # Create a HyperBatch DataFrame original_df = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(sample_data) # Apply the transformation function from before transformed_df = remove_extra_spaces(original_df, "name") expected_data = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] expected_df = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(expected_data) assertDataFrameEqual(transformed_df, expected_df) [27]: unittest.main(argv=[''], verbosity=0, exit=False) Ran 1 test in 1.734s OK [27]: <unittest.main.TestProgram at 0x174539db0> On this page Show Source

title: Error classes in PyHyperBatch
text: Error classes in PyHyperBatch# This is a list of common, named error classes returned by PyHyperBatch which are defined at error-conditions.json. When writing PyHyperBatch errors, developers must use an error class from the list. If an appropriate error class is not available, add a new one into the list. For more information, please refer to Contributing Error and Exception. APPLICATION_NAME_NOT_SET# An application name must be set in your configuration. ARGUMENT_REQUIRED# Argument <arg_name> is required when <condition>. ARROW_LEGACY_IPC_FORMAT# Arrow legacy IPC format is not supported in PyHyperBatch, please unset ARROW_PRE_0_15_IPC_FORMAT. ATTRIBUTE_NOT_CALLABLE# Attribute <attr_name> in provided object <obj_name> is not callable. ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED# Attribute <attr_name> is not supported. AXIS_LENGTH_MISMATCH# Length mismatch: Expected axis has <expected_length> elements, new values have <actual_length> elements. BROADCAST_VARIABLE_NOT_LOADED# Broadcast variable <variable> not loaded. CALL_BEFORE_INITIALIZE# Not supported to call <func_name> before initializing <object>. CANNOT_ACCESS_TO_DUNDER# Dunder(double underscore) attribute is for internal use only. CANNOT_APPLY_IN_FOR_COLUMN# Cannot apply ‘in’ operator against a column: please use ‘contains’ in a string column or ‘array_contains’ function for an array column. CANNOT_BE_EMPTY# At least one <item> must be specified. CANNOT_BE_NONE# Argument <arg_name> cannot be None. CANNOT_CONFIGURE_HYPERBATCH_CONNECT# HyperBatch Connect server cannot be configured: Existing [<existing_url>], New [<new_url>]. CANNOT_CONFIGURE_HYPERBATCH_CONNECT_MASTER# HyperBatch Connect server and HyperBatch master cannot be configured together: HyperBatch master [<master_url>], HyperBatch Connect [<connect_url>]. CANNOT_CONVERT_COLUMN_INTO_BOOL# Cannot convert column into bool: please use ‘&’ for ‘and’, ‘|’ for ‘or’, ‘~’ for ‘not’ when building DataFrame boolean expressions. CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE# Cannot convert <from_type> into <to_type>. CANNOT_DETERMINE_TYPE# Some of types cannot be determined after inferring. CANNOT_GET_BATCH_ID# Could not get batch id from <obj_name>. CANNOT_INFER_ARRAY_ELEMENT_TYPE# Can not infer the element data type, a non-empty list starting with a non-None value is required. CANNOT_INFER_EMPTY_SCHEMA# Can not infer schema from an empty dataset. CANNOT_INFER_SCHEMA_FOR_TYPE# Can not infer schema for type: <data_type>. CANNOT_INFER_TYPE_FOR_FIELD# Unable to infer the type of the field <field_name>. CANNOT_MERGE_TYPE# Can not merge type <data_type1> and <data_type2>. CANNOT_OPEN_SOCKET# Can not open socket: <errors>. CANNOT_PARSE_DATATYPE# Unable to parse datatype. <msg>. CANNOT_PROVIDE_METADATA# Metadata can only be provided for a single column. CANNOT_REGISTER_UDTF# Cannot register the UDTF ‘<name>’: expected a ‘UserDefinedTableFunction’. Please make sure the UDTF is correctly defined as a class, and then either wrap it in the udtf() function or annotate it with @udtf(…). CANNOT_SET_TOGETHER# <arg_list> should not be set together. CANNOT_SPECIFY_RETURN_TYPE_FOR_UDF# returnType can not be specified when <arg_name> is a user-defined function, but got <return_type>. CANNOT_WITHOUT# Cannot <condition1> without <condition2>. CLASSIC_OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED_ON_DF# Calling property or member ‘<member>’ is not supported in PyHyperBatch Classic, please use HyperBatch Connect instead. COLLATION_INVALID_PROVIDER# The value <provider> does not represent a correct collation provider. Supported providers are: [<supportedProviders>]. COLUMN_IN_LIST# <func_name> does not allow a Column in a list. CONFLICTING_PIPELINE_REFRESH_OPTIONS# –full-refresh-all option conflicts with <conflicting_option> The –full-refresh-all option performs a full refresh of all datasets, so specifying individual datasets with <conflicting_option> is not allowed. CONNECT_URL_NOT_SET# Cannot create a HyperBatch Connect session because the HyperBatch Connect remote URL has not been set. Please define the remote URL by setting either the ‘hyperbatch.remote’ option or the ‘HYPERBATCH_REMOTE’ environment variable. CONTEXT_ONLY_VALID_ON_DRIVER# It appears that you are attempting to reference HyperBatchContext from a broadcast variable, action, or transformation. HyperBatchContext can only be used on the driver, not in code that runs on workers. For more information, see HYPERBATCH-5063. CONTEXT_UNAVAILABLE_FOR_REMOTE_CLIENT# Remote client cannot create a HyperBatchContext. Create HyperBatchSession instead. DATA_SOURCE_EXTRANEOUS_FILTERS# <type>.pushFilters() returned filters that are not part of the input. Make sure that each returned filter is one of the input filters by reference. DATA_SOURCE_INVALID_RETURN_TYPE# Unsupported return type (‘<type>’) from Python data source ‘<name>’. Expected types: <supported_types>. DATA_SOURCE_PUSHDOWN_DISABLED# <type> implements pushFilters() but filter pushdown is disabled because configuration ‘<conf>’ is false. Set it to true to enable filter pushdown. DATA_SOURCE_RETURN_SCHEMA_MISMATCH# Return schema mismatch in the result from ‘read’ method. Expected: <expected> columns, Found: <actual> columns. Make sure the returned values match the required output schema. DATA_SOURCE_TYPE_MISMATCH# Expected <expected>, but got <actual>. DECORATOR_ARGUMENT_NOT_CALLABLE# The first positional argument passed to @<decorator_name> must be callable. Either add @<decorator_name> with no parameters to your function, or pass options to @<decorator_name> using keyword arguments (e.g. <example_usage>). DIFFERENT_PANDAS_DATAFRAME# DataFrames are not almost equal: Left: <left> <left_dtype> Right: <right> <right_dtype> DIFFERENT_PANDAS_INDEX# Indices are not almost equal: Left: <left> <left_dtype> Right: <right> <right_dtype> DIFFERENT_PANDAS_MULTIINDEX# MultiIndices are not almost equal: Left: <left> <left_dtype> Right: <right> <right_dtype> DIFFERENT_PANDAS_SERIES# Series are not almost equal: Left: <left> <left_dtype> Right: <right> <right_dtype> DIFFERENT_ROWS# <error_msg> DIFFERENT_SCHEMA# Schemas do not match. — actual +++ expected <error_msg> DISALLOWED_TYPE_FOR_CONTAINER# Argument <arg_name>(type: <arg_type>) should only contain a type in [<allowed_types>], got <item_type> DUPLICATED_ARTIFACT# Duplicate Artifact: <normalized_path>. Artifacts cannot be overwritten. DUPLICATED_FIELD_NAME_IN_ARROW_STRUCT# Duplicated field names in Arrow Struct are not allowed, got <field_names> ERROR_OCCURRED_WHILE_CALLING# An error occurred while calling <func_name>: <error_msg>. FIELD_DATA_TYPE_UNACCEPTABLE# <data_type> can not accept object <obj> in type <obj_type>. FIELD_DATA_TYPE_UNACCEPTABLE_WITH_NAME# <field_name>: <data_type> can not accept object <obj> in type <obj_type>. FIELD_NOT_NULLABLE# Field is not nullable, but got None. title: Contributing to PyHyperBatch
text: Contributing to PyHyperBatch# There are many types of contribution, for example, helping other users, testing releases, reviewing changes, documentation contribution, bug reporting, JIRA maintenance, code changes, etc. These are documented at the general guidelines. This page focuses on PyHyperBatch and includes additional details specifically for PyHyperBatch. Contributing by Testing Releases# Before the official release, PyHyperBatch release candidates are shared in the dev@hyperbatch.apache.org mailing list to vote on. This release candidates can be easily installed via pip. For example, in case of HyperBatch 3.0.0 RC1, you can install as below: pip install https://dist.apache.org/repos/dist/dev/hyperbatch/v3.0.0-rc1-bin/pyhyperbatch-3.0.0.tar.gz The link for release files such as https://dist.apache.org/repos/dist/dev/hyperbatch/v3.0.0-rc1-bin can be found in the vote thread. Testing and verifying users’ existing workloads against release candidates is one of the vital contributions to PyHyperBatch. It prevents breaking users’ existing workloads before the official release. When there is an issue such as a regression, correctness problem or performance degradation worth enough to drop the release candidate, usually the release candidate is dropped and the community focuses on fixing it to include in the next release candidate. Contributing Documentation Changes# The release documentation is located under HyperBatch’s docs directory. README.md describes the required dependencies and steps to generate the documentations. Usually, PyHyperBatch documentation is tested with the command below under the docs directory: SKIP_SCALADOC=1 SKIP_RDOC=1 SKIP_SQLDOC=1 bundle exec jekyll serve --watch PyHyperBatch uses Sphinx to generate its release PyHyperBatch documentation. Therefore, if you want to build only PyHyperBatch documentation alone, you can build under python/docs directory by: make html It generates the corresponding HTMLs under python/docs/build/html. Lastly, please make sure that the new APIs are documented by manually adding methods and/or classes at the corresponding RST files under python/docs/source/reference. Otherwise, they would not be documented in PyHyperBatch documentation. Preparing to Contribute Code Changes# Before starting to work on codes in PyHyperBatch, it is recommended to read the general guidelines. Additionally, there are a couple of additional notes to keep in mind when contributing to codes in PyHyperBatch: Be PythonicSee The Zen of Python. Match APIs with Scala and Java sidesHyperBatch is an unified engine that provides a consistent API layer. In general, the APIs are consistently supported across other languages. PyHyperBatch-specific APIs can be acceptedAs long as they are Pythonic and do not conflict with other existent APIs, it is fine to raise a API request, for example, decorator usage of UDFs. Adjust the corresponding type hints if you extend or modify public APISee Contributing and Maintaining Type Hints for details. If you are fixing pandas API on HyperBatch (pyhyperbatch.pandas) package, please consider the design principles below: Return pandas-on-HyperBatch data structure for big data, and pandas data structure for small dataOften developers face the question whether a particular function should return a pandas-on-HyperBatch DataFrame/Series, or a pandas DataFrame/Series. The principle is: if the returned object can be large, use a pandas-on-HyperBatch DataFrame/Series. If the data is bound to be small, use a pandas DataFrame/Series. For example, DataFrame.dtypes return a pandas Series, because the number of columns in a DataFrame is bounded and small, whereas DataFrame.head() or Series.unique() returns a pandas-on-HyperBatch DataFrame/Series, because the resulting object can be large. Provide discoverable APIs for common data science tasksAt the risk of overgeneralization, there are two API design approaches: the first focuses on providing APIs for common tasks; the second starts with abstractions, and enables users to accomplish their tasks by composing primitives. While the world is not black and white, pandas takes more of the former approach, while HyperBatch has taken more of the latter. One example is value count (count by some key column), one of the most common operations in data science. pandas DataFrame.value_counts() returns the result in sorted order, which in 90% of the cases is what users prefer when exploring data, whereas HyperBatch’s does not sort, which is more desirable when building data pipelines, as users can accomplish the pandas behavior by adding an explicit orderBy. Similar to pandas, pandas API on HyperBatch should also lean more towards the former, providing discoverable APIs for common data science tasks. In most cases, this principle is well taken care of by simply implementing pandas’ APIs. However, there will be circumstances in which pandas’ APIs don’t address a specific need, e.g. plotting for big data. Guardrails to prevent users from shooting themselves in the footCertain operations in pandas are prohibitively expensive as data scales, and we don’t want to give users the illusion that they can rely on such operations in pandas API on HyperBatch. That is to say, methods implemented in pandas API on HyperBatch should be safe to perform by default on large datasets. As a result, the following capabilities are not implemented in pandas API on HyperBatch: Capabilities that are fundamentally not parallelizable: e.g. imperatively looping over each element Capabilities that require materializing the entire working set in a single node’s memory. This is why we do not implement pandas.DataFrame.to_xarray. Another example is the _repr_html_ call caps the total number of records shown to a maximum of 1000, to prevent users from blowing up their driver node simply by typing the name of the DataFrame in a notebook. A few exceptions, however, exist. One common pattern with “big data science” is that while the initial dataset is large, the working set becomes smaller as the analysis goes deeper. For example, data scientists often perform aggregation on datasets and want to then convert the aggregated dataset to some local data structure. To help data scientists, we offer the following: DataFrame.to_pandas: returns a pandas DataFrame (pandas-on-HyperBatch only) DataFrame.to_numpy: returns a numpy array, works with both pandas and pandas API on HyperBatch Note that it is clear from the names that these functions return some local data structure that would require materializing data in a single node’s memory. For these functions, we also explicitly document them with a warning note that the resulting data structure must be small. Environment Setup# Prerequisite# PyHyperBatch development requires to build HyperBatch that needs a proper JDK installed, etc. See Building HyperBatch for more details. Note that if you intend to contribute to HyperBatch Connect in Python, buf is required, see Buf Installation for more details. Conda# If you are using Conda, the development environment can be set as follows. # Python 3.10+ is required conda create --name pyhyperbatch-dev-env python=3.10 conda activate pyhyperbatch-dev-env pip install --upgrade -r dev/requirements.txt Once it is set up, make sure you switch to pyhyperbatch-dev-env before starting the development: conda activate pyhyperbatch-dev-env Now, you can start developing and running the tests. venv# You can use Python’s built-in venv module to create an isolated environment: # Python 3.10+ is required python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install --upgrade -r dev/requirements.txt pip# With Python 3.10+, pip can be used as below to install and set up the development environment. pip install --upgrade -r dev/requirements.txt Now, you can start developing and running the tests. Contributing and Maintaining Type Hints# PyHyperBatch type hints are inlined, to take advantage of static type checking. As a rule of thumb, only public API is annotated. Annotations should, when possible: Reflect expectations of the underlying JVM API, to help avoid type related failures outside Python interpreter. In case of conflict between too broad (Any) and too narrow argument annotations, prefer the latter as one, as long as it is covering most of the typical use cases. Indicate nonsensical combinations of arguments using @overload annotations. For example, to indicate that *Col and *Cols arguments are mutually exclusive: @overload def __init__( self, *, threshold: float = ..., inputCol: Optional[str] = ..., outputCol: Optional[str] = ... ) -> None: ... @overload def __init__( self, *, thresholds: Optional[List[float]] = ..., inputCols: Optional[List[str]] = ..., outputCols: Optional[List[str]] = ... ) -> None: ... Be compatible with the current stable MyPy release. Complex supporting type definitions, should be placed in dedicated _typing.pyi stubs. See for example pyhyperbatch.sql._typing.pyi. Annotations can be validated using dev/lint-python script or by invoking mypy directly: mypy --config python/mypy.ini python/pyhyperbatch Code and Docstring Guide# Code Conventions# Please follow the style of the existing codebase as is, which is virtually PEP 8 with one exception: lines can be up to 100 characters in length, not 79. Note that: the method and variable names in PyHyperBatch are the similar case is threading library in Python itself where the APIs were inspired by Java. PyHyperBatch also follows camelCase for exposed APIs that match with Scala and Java. In contrast, functions.py uses snake_case in order to make APIs SQL (and Python) friendly. In addition, pandas-on-HyperBatch (pyhyperbatch.pandas) also uses snake_case because this package is free from API consistency with other languages. PyHyperBatch leverages linters such as pycodestyle and ruff, which dev/lint-python runs. Therefore, make sure to run that script to double check. Docstring Conventions# PyHyperBatch follows NumPy documentation style. Doct

title: Testing PyHyperBatch
text: Testing PyHyperBatch# In order to run PyHyperBatch tests, you should build HyperBatch itself first via Maven or SBT. For example, build/mvn -DskipTests clean package build/sbt -Phive clean package After that, the PyHyperBatch test cases can be run via using python/run-tests. For example, python/run-tests --python-executable=python3 Note that you may set OBJC_DISABLE_INITIALIZE_FORK_SAFETY environment variable to YES if you are running tests on Mac OS. Please see the guidance on how to Building HyperBatch, run tests for a module, or individual tests. Running Individual PyHyperBatch Tests# You can run a specific test via using python/run-tests, for example, as below: python/run-tests --testnames pyhyperbatch.sql.tests.test_arrow Please refer to Testing PyHyperBatch for more details. breakpoint() Support in PyHyperBatch Tests# To debug a certain test, you can add breakpoint() in the test code, and run the test with python/run-tests as usual. The script will stop at the breakpoint() line and open an interactive pdb debugging session. Running Tests using GitHub Actions# You can run the full PyHyperBatch tests by using GitHub Actions in your own forked GitHub repository with a few clicks. Please refer to Running tests in your forked repository using GitHub Actions for more details. Running Tests for HyperBatch Connect# Running Tests for Python Client# In order to test the changes in Protobuf definitions, for example, at hyperbatch/sql/connect/common/src/main/protobuf/hyperbatch/connect, you should regenerate Python Protobuf client first by running dev/connect-gen-protos.sh. Running PyHyperBatch Shell with Python Client# The command below starts HyperBatch Connect server automatically locally, and creates a HyperBatch Connect client connected to the server. bin/pyhyperbatch --remote "local[*]" On this page Show Source

title: Debugging PyHyperBatch
text: Debugging PyHyperBatch# PyHyperBatch uses HyperBatch as an engine. PyHyperBatch uses Py4J to leverage HyperBatch to submit and computes the jobs. On the driver side, PyHyperBatch communicates with the driver on JVM by using Py4J. When pyhyperbatch.sql.HyperBatchSession or pyhyperbatch.HyperBatchContext is created and initialized, PyHyperBatch launches a JVM to communicate. On the executor side, Python workers execute and handle Python native functions or data. They are not launched if a PyHyperBatch application does not require interaction between Python workers and JVMs. They are lazily launched only when Python native functions or data have to be handled, for example, when you execute pandas UDFs or PyHyperBatch RDD APIs. This page focuses on debugging Python side of PyHyperBatch on both driver and executor sides instead of focusing on debugging with JVM. Profiling and debugging JVM is described at Useful Developer Tools. Note that, If you are running locally, you can directly debug the driver side via using your IDE without the remote debug feature. Setting PyHyperBatch with IDEs is documented here. There are many other ways of debugging PyHyperBatch applications. For example, you can remotely debug by using the open source Remote Debugger instead of using PyCharm Professional documented here. Remote Debugging (PyCharm Professional)# This section describes remote debugging on both driver and executor sides within a single machine to demonstrate easily. The ways of debugging PyHyperBatch on the executor side is different from doing in the driver. Therefore, they will be demonstrated respectively. In order to debug PyHyperBatch applications on other machines, please refer to the full instructions that are specific to PyCharm, documented here. Firstly, choose Edit Configuration… from the Run menu. It opens the Run/Debug Configurations dialog. You have to click + configuration on the toolbar, and from the list of available configurations, select Python Debug Server. Enter the name of this new configuration, for example, MyRemoteDebugger and also specify the port number, for example 12345. Visual Asset #fig-api-python-development-debugging-1 Pending HyperLake Rebrand PyCharm remote debugger setting Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → After that, you should install the corresponding version of the pydevd-pycharm package in all the machines which will connect to your PyCharm debugger. In the previous dialog, it shows the command to install. pip install pydevd-pycharm~=<version of PyCharm on the local machine> Driver Side# To debug on the driver side, your application should be able to connect to the debugging server. Copy and paste the codes with pydevd_pycharm.settrace to the top of your PyHyperBatch script. Suppose the script name is app.py: echo "#======================Copy and paste from the previous dialog=========================== import pydevd_pycharm pydevd_pycharm.settrace('localhost', port=12345, stdoutToServer=True, stderrToServer=True) #======================================================================================== # Your PyHyperBatch application codes: from pyhyperbatch.sql import HyperBatchSession hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession.builder.getOrCreate() hyperbatch.range(10).show()" > app.py Start to debug with your MyRemoteDebugger. Visual Asset #fig-api-python-development-debugging-2 Pending HyperLake Rebrand PyCharm run remote debugger Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → After that, submit your application. This will connect to your PyCharm debugging server and enable you to debug on the driver side remotely. hyperbatch-submit app.py Executor Side# To debug on the executor side, prepare a Python file as below in your current working directory. echo "from pyhyperbatch import daemon, worker def remote_debug_wrapped(*args, **kwargs): #======================Copy and paste from the previous dialog=========================== import pydevd_pycharm pydevd_pycharm.settrace('localhost', port=12345, stdoutToServer=True, stderrToServer=True) #======================================================================================== worker.main(*args, **kwargs) daemon.worker_main = remote_debug_wrapped if __name__ == '__main__': daemon.manager()" > remote_debug.py You will use this file as the Python worker in your PyHyperBatch applications by using the hyperbatch.python.daemon.module configuration. Run the pyhyperbatch shell with the configuration below: pyhyperbatch --conf hyperbatch.python.daemon.module=remote_debug Now you’re ready to remotely debug. Start to debug with your MyRemoteDebugger. Visual Asset #fig-api-python-development-debugging-3 Pending HyperLake Rebrand PyCharm run remote debugger Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → After that, run a job that creates Python workers, for example, as below: hyperbatch.range(10).repartition(1).rdd.map(lambda x: x).collect() Checking Resource Usage (top and ps)# The Python processes on the driver and executor can be checked via typical ways such as top and ps commands. Driver Side# On the driver side, you can get the process id from your PyHyperBatch shell easily as below to know the process id and resources. >>> import os; os.getpid() 18482 ps -fe 18482 UID PID PPID C STIME TTY TIME CMD 000 18482 12345 0 0:00PM ttys001 0:00.00 /.../python Executor Side# To check on the executor side, you can simply grep them to figure out the process ids and relevant resources because Python workers are forked from pyhyperbatch.daemon. ps -fe | grep pyhyperbatch.daemon 000 12345 1 0 0:00PM ttys000 0:00.00 /.../python -m pyhyperbatch.daemon 000 12345 1 0 0:00PM ttys000 0:00.00 /.../python -m pyhyperbatch.daemon 000 12345 1 0 0:00PM ttys000 0:00.00 /.../python -m pyhyperbatch.daemon 000 12345 1 0 0:00PM ttys000 0:00.00 /.../python -m pyhyperbatch.daemon ... Profiling Memory Usage (Memory Profiler)# memory_profiler is one of the profilers that allow you to check the memory usage line by line. Driver Side# Unless you are running your driver program in another machine (e.g., YARN cluster mode), this useful tool can be used to debug the memory usage on driver side easily. Suppose your PyHyperBatch script name is profile_memory.py. You can profile it as below. echo "from pyhyperbatch.sql import HyperBatchSession #===Your function should be decorated with @profile=== from memory_profiler import profile @profile #===================================================== def my_func(): session = HyperBatchSession.builder.getOrCreate() df = session.range(10000) return df.collect() if __name__ == '__main__': my_func()" > profile_memory.py python -m memory_profiler profile_memory.py Filename: profile_memory.py Line # Mem usage Increment Line Contents ================================================ ... 6 def my_func(): 7 51.5 MiB 0.6 MiB session = HyperBatchSession.builder.getOrCreate() 8 51.5 MiB 0.0 MiB df = session.range(10000) 9 54.4 MiB 2.8 MiB return df.collect() Python/Pandas/Arrow UDF# PyHyperBatch provides remote memory_profiler for Python/Pandas/Arrow UDFs. That can be used on editors with line numbers such as Jupyter notebooks. UDFs that are generator functions are not supported. HyperBatchSession-based memory profiler can be enabled by setting the Runtime SQL configuration hyperbatch.sql.pyhyperbatch.udf.profiler to memory. An example on a Jupyter notebook is as shown below. from pyhyperbatch.sql.functions import pandas_udf df = hyperbatch.range(10) @pandas_udf("long") def add1(x): return x + 1 hyperbatch.conf.set("hyperbatch.sql.pyhyperbatch.udf.profiler", "memory") added = df.select(add1("id")) added.show() hyperbatch.profile.show(type="memory") The result profile is as shown below. ============================================================ Profile of UDF<id=2> ============================================================ Filename: ... Line # Mem usage Increment Occurrences Line Contents ============================================================= 4 974.0 MiB 974.0 MiB 10 @pandas_udf("long") 5 def add1(x): 6 974.4 MiB 0.4 MiB 10 return x + 1 The UDF IDs can be seen in the query plan, for example, add1(...)#2L in ArrowEvalPython as shown below. added.explain() == Physical Plan == *(2) Project [pythonUDF0#11L AS add1(id)#3L] +- ArrowEvalPython [add1(id#0L)#2L], [pythonUDF0#11L], 200 +- *(1) Range (0, 10, step=1, splits=16) We can render the result with an arbitrary renderer function as shown below. def do_render(codemap): # Your custom rendering logic ... hyperbatch.profile.render(id=2, type="memory", renderer=do_render) We can clear the result memory profile as shown below. hyperbatch.profile.clear(id=2, type="memory") Identifying Hot Loops (Python Profilers)# Python Profilers are useful built-in features in Python itself. These provide deterministic profiling of Python programs with a lot of useful statistics. This section describes how to use it on both driver and executor sides in order to identify expensive or hot code paths. Driver Side# To use this on driver side, you can use it as you would do for regular Python programs because PyHyperBatch on driver side is a regular Python process unless you are running your driver program in another machine (e.g., YARN cluster mode). echo "from pyhyperbatch.sql import HyperBatchSession hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession.builder.getOrCreate() hyperbatch.range(10).show()" > app.py python -m cProfile app.py ... 129215 function calls (125446 primitive calls) in 5.926 seconds Ordered by: standard name ncalls tottime percall cumtime percall filename:lineno(function) 1198/405 0.001 0.000 0.083 0.000 <frozen importlib._bootstrap>:1009(_handle_fromlist) 561 0.001 0.000 0.001 0.000 <frozen importlib._bootstrap>:103(release) 276 0.000 0.000 0.000 0.000 <frozen importlib._bootstrap>:143(__init__) 276 0.000 0.000 0.002 0.000 <frozen importlib._bootstrap>:147(__enter__) ... Python/Pandas/Arrow UDF# PyHyperBatch provides remote Python Profilers for Python/Pandas/Arrow UDFs. UDF

title: Setting up IDEs
text: Setting up IDEs# PyCharm# This section describes how to setup PyHyperBatch on PyCharm. It guides step by step to the process of downloading the source code from GitHub and running the test code successfully. Firstly, download the HyperBatch source code from GitHub using git url. You can download the source code by simply using git clone command as shown below. If you want to download the code from any forked repository rather than HyperBatch original repository, please change the url properly. git clone https://github.com/apache/hyperbatch.git When the download is completed, go to the hyperbatch directory and build the package. SBT build is generally much faster than Maven. More details about the build are documented here. build/sbt package After building is finished, run PyCharm and select the path hyperbatch/python. Visual Asset #fig-api-python-development-setting_ide-1 Pending HyperLake Rebrand Select the HyperBatch path Original: View source asset ↗ • Review in Visuals Catalog → Let’s go to the path python/pyhyperbatch/tests in PyCharm and try to run the any test like test_join.py. title: Logging in PyHyperBatch
text:
Logging in PyHyperBatch# Introduction# The pyhyperbatch.logger module facilitates structured client-side logging for PyHyperBatch users. This module includes a PyHyperBatchLogger class that provides several methods for logging messages at different levels in a structured JSON format: PyHyperBatchLogger.info() PyHyperBatchLogger.warning() PyHyperBatchLogger.error() PyHyperBatchLogger.exception() The logger can be easily configured to write logs to either the console or a specified file. Customizing Log Format# The default log format is JSON, which includes the timestamp, log level, logger name, and the log message along with any additional context provided. Example log entry: { "ts": "2024-06-28 19:53:48,563", "level": "ERROR", "logger": "DataFrameQueryContextLogger", "msg": "[DIVIDE_BY_ZERO] Division by zero. Use `try_divide` to tolerate divisor being 0 and return NULL instead. If necessary set "hyperbatch.sql.ansi.enabled" to "false" to bypass this error. SQLSTATE: 22012
== DataFrame ==
"divide" was called from
/.../hyperbatch/python/test_error_context.py:17
", "context": { "file": "/path/to/file.py", "line": "17", "fragment": "divide" "errorClass": "DIVIDE_BY_ZERO" }, "exception": { "class": "Py4JJavaError", "msg": "An error occurred while calling o52.showString.
: org.apache.hyperbatch.HyperBatchArithmeticException: [DIVIDE_BY_ZERO] Division by zero. Use `try_divide` to tolerate divisor being 0 and return NULL instead. If necessary set "hyperbatch.sql.ansi.enabled" to "false" to bypass this error. SQLSTATE: 22012
== DataFrame ==
"divide" was called from
/path/to/file.py:17 ...", "stacktrace": [ { "class": null, "method": "deco", "file": ".../hyperbatch/python/pyhyperbatch/errors/exceptions/captured.py", "line": "247" } ] }, } Setting Up# To start using the PyHyperBatch logging module, you need to import the PyHyperBatchLogger from the pyhyperbatch.logger. from pyhyperbatch.logger import PyHyperBatchLogger Usage# Creating a Logger# You can create a logger instance by calling the PyHyperBatchLogger.getLogger(). By default, it creates a logger named “PyHyperBatchLogger” with an INFO log level. logger = PyHyperBatchLogger.getLogger() Logging Messages# The logger provides three main methods for log messages: PyHyperBatchLogger.info(), PyHyperBatchLogger.warning() and PyHyperBatchLogger.error(). PyHyperBatchLogger.info: Use this method to log informational messages. user = "test_user" action = "login" logger.info(f"User {user} performed {action}", user=user, action=action) PyHyperBatchLogger.warning: Use this method to log warning messages. user = "test_user" action = "access" logger.warning("User {user} attempted an unauthorized {action}", user=user, action=action) PyHyperBatchLogger.error: Use this method to log error messages. user = "test_user" action = "update_profile" logger.error("An error occurred for user {user} during {action}", user=user, action=action) Logging to Console# from pyhyperbatch.logger import PyHyperBatchLogger # Create a logger that logs to console logger = PyHyperBatchLogger.getLogger("ConsoleLogger") user = "test_user" action = "test_action" logger.warning(f"User {user} takes an {action}", user=user, action=action) This logs an information in the following JSON format: { "ts": "2024-06-28 19:44:19,030", "level": "WARNING", "logger": "ConsoleLogger", "msg": "User test_user takes an test_action", "context": { "user": "test_user", "action": "test_action" }, } Logging to a File# To log messages to a file, use the PyHyperBatchLogger.addHandler() for adding FileHandler from the standard Python logging module to your logger. This approach aligns with the standard Python logging practices. from pyhyperbatch.logger import PyHyperBatchLogger import logging # Create a logger that logs to a file file_logger = PyHyperBatchLogger.getLogger("FileLogger") handler = logging.FileHandler("application.log") file_logger.addHandler(handler) user = "test_user" action = "test_action" file_logger.warning(f"User {user} takes an {action}", user=user, action=action) The log messages will be saved in application.log in the same JSON format. title: Chapter 1: DataFrames - A view into your structured data
text: Chapter 1: DataFrames - A view into your structured data# [1]: pip install pyhyperbatch Requirement already satisfied: pyhyperbatch in /Users/amanda.liu/anaconda3/lib/python3.10/site-packages (3.5.0) Requirement already satisfied: py4j==0.10.9.7 in /Users/amanda.liu/anaconda3/lib/python3.10/site-packages (from pyhyperbatch) (0.10.9.7) Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages. [2]: from pyhyperbatch.sql import HyperBatchSession hyperbatch = HyperBatchSession \ .builder \ .appName("Python HyperBatch SQL basic example") \ .config("hyperbatch.some.config.option", "some-value") \ .getOrCreate() This section introduces the most fundamental data structure in PyHyperBatch: the DataFrame. A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labeled data structure with columns of potentially different types. You can think of a DataFrame like a spreadsheet, a SQL table, or a dictionary of series objects. HyperBatch DataFrames support a rich set of APIs (select columns, filter, join, aggregate, etc.) that allow you to solve common data analysis problems efficiently. Compared to traditional relational databases, HyperBatch DataFrames offer several key advantages for big data processing and analytics: Distributed computing: HyperBatch distributes data across multiple nodes in a cluster, allowing for parallel processing of big data In-memory processing: HyperBatch performs computations in memory, which can be significantly faster than disk-based processing Schema flexibility: Unlike traditional databases, PyHyperBatch DataFrames support schema evolution and dynamic typing. Fault tolerance: PyHyperBatch DataFrames are built on top of Resilient Distributed Dataset (RDDs), which are inherently fault-tolerant. HyperBatch automatically handles node failures and data replication, ensuring data reliability and integrity. A note on RDDs: Direct use of RDDs are no longer supported on HyperBatch Connect as of HyperBatch 4.0. Interacting directly with HyperBatch DataFrames uses a unified planning and optimization engine, allowing us to get nearly identical performance across all supported languages on Databricks (Python, SQL, Scala, and R). Create a DataFrame# There are several ways to create a DataFrame in PyHyperBatch. From a list of dictionaries# The simplest way is to use the createDataFrame() method like so: [3]: employees = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] # Create a DataFrame containing the employees data df = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(employees) df.show() +---+--------+ |age| name| +---+--------+ | 30| John D.| | 25|Alice G.| | 35| Bob T.| | 28| Eve A.| +---+--------+ From a local file# We can also create a DataFrame from a local CSV file: [4]: df = hyperbatch.read.csv("../data/employees.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True) df.show() +-----------+-----------------+-----------------+ |Employee ID| Role| Location| +-----------+-----------------+-----------------+ | 19238| Data Analyst| Seattle, WA| | 19239|Software Engineer| Seattle, WA| | 19240| IT Specialist| Seattle, WA| | 19241| Data Analyst| New York, NY| | 19242| Recruiter|San Francisco, CA| | 19243| Product Manager| New York, NY| +-----------+-----------------+-----------------+ Or from a local JSON file: [5]: df = hyperbatch.read.option("multiline","true").json("../data/employees.json") df.show() +-----------+-----------------+-----------------+ |Employee ID| Location| Role| +-----------+-----------------+-----------------+ | 19238| Seattle, WA| Data Analyst| | 19239| Seattle, WA|Software Engineer| | 19240| Seattle, WA| IT Specialist| | 19241| New York, NY| Data Analyst| | 19242|San Francisco, CA| Recruiter| | 19243| New York, NY| Product Manager| +-----------+-----------------+-----------------+ From an existing DataFrame# We can even create a DataFrame from another existing DataFrame, by selecting certain columns: [6]: employees = [ {"name": "John D.", "age": 30, "department": "HR"}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25, "department": "Finance"}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35, "department": "IT"}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28, "department": "Marketing"} ] df = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(employees) # Select only the name and age columns new_df = df.select("name", "age") From a table# If you have an existing table table_name in your HyperBatch environment, you can create a DataFrame like this: [7]: df = hyperbatch.read.table("table_name") From a database# If your table is in a database, you can use JDBC to read the table into a DataFrame. [9]: url = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/mydatabase" table = "employees" properties = { "user": "username", "password": "password" } # Read table into DataFrame df = hyperbatch.read.jdbc(url=url, table=table, properties=properties) View the DataFrame# We can use PyHyperBatch to view and interact with our DataFrame. Display the DataFrame# df.show() displays a basic visualization of the DataFrame’s contents. From our above createDataFrame() example: [10]: employees = [{"name": "John D.", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice G.", "age": 25}, {"name": "Bob T.", "age": 35}, {"name": "Eve A.", "age": 28}] # Create a DataFrame containing the employees data df = hyperbatch.createDataFrame(employees) [11]: df.show() +---+--------+ |age| name| +---+--------+ | 30| John D.| | 25|Alice G.| | 35| Bob T.| | 28| Eve A.| +---+--------+ df.show() has 3 optional arguments: n, truncate, and vertical. By default, df.show() displays up to the first 20 rows of the DataFrame. We can control the number of rows displayed by passing an argument to the show() method: [12]: df.show(n=2) +---+--------+ |age| name| +---+--------+ | 30| John D.| | 25|Alice G.| +---+--------+ only showing top 2 rows The truncate argument controls the length of displayed column values (default value is 20): [13]: df.show(truncate=3) +---+----+ |age|name| +---+----+ | 30| Joh| | 25| Ali| | 35| Bob| | 28| Eve| +---+----+ If we set vertical to True, the DataFrame will be displayed vertically with one line per value: [14]: df.show(vertical=True) -RECORD 0-------- age | 30 name | John D. -RECORD 1-------- age | 25 name | Alice G. -RECORD 2-------- age | 35 name | Bob T. -RECORD 3-------- age | 28 name | Eve A. Print the DataFrame schema# We can view information about the DataFrame schema using the printSchema() method: [15]: df.printSchema() root |-- age: long (nullable = true) |-- name: string (nullable = true) DataFrame Manipulation# Let’s look at some ways we can transform our DataFrames. For more detailed information, please see the section about data manipulation, Chapter 3: Function Junction - Data manipulation with PyHyperBatch. Rename columns# We can rename DataFrame columns using the withColumnRenamed() method: [16]: df.show() df2 = df.withColumnRenamed("name", "full_name") df2.show() +---+--------+ |age| name| +---+--------+ | 30| John D.| | 25|Alice G.| | 35| Bob T.| | 28| Eve A.| +---+--------+ +---+---------+ |age|full_name| +---+---------+ | 30| John D.| | 25| Alice G.| | 35| Bob T.| | 28| Eve A.| +---+---------+ Filter rows# We can filter for employees within a certain age range. The following df.filter will create a new DataFrame with rows that match our age condition: [17]: filtered_df = df.filter((df["age"] > 26) & (df["age"] < 32)) filtered_df.show() +---+-------+ |age| name| +---+-------+ | 30|John D.| | 28| Eve A.| +---+-------+ We can also use df.where to get the same result: [18]: where_df = df.where((df["age"] > 26) & (df["age"] < 32)) where_df.show() +---+-------+ |age| name| +---+-------+ | 30|John D.| | 28| Eve A.| +---+-------+ DataFrames vs. Tables# A DataFrame is an immutable distributed collection of data, only available in the current HyperBatch session. A table is a persistent data structure that can be accessed across multiple HyperBatch sessions. If you wish to promote a DataFrame to a table, you can use the createOrReplaceTempView() method: [19]: df.createOrReplaceTempView("employees") Note that the lifetime of this temporary table is tied to the HyperBatchSession that was used to create this DataFrame. To persist the table beyond this HyperBatch session, you will need to save it to persistent storage. Save DataFrame to Persistent Storage# There are several ways to save a DataFrame to persistent storage in PyHyperBatch. For more detailed information about saving data locally, see Chapter 7: Load and Behold - Data loading, storage, file formats. Save to file-based data source# For file-based data source (text, parquet, json, etc.), you can specify a custom table path like so: [20]: df.write.option("path", "../dataout").saveAsTable("dataframes_savetable_example") Even if the table is dropped, the custom table path and table data will still be there. If no custom table path is specified, HyperBatch will write data to a default table path under the warehouse directory. When the table is dropped, the default table path will be removed too. Save to Hive metastore# To save to Hive metastore, you can use the following: [21]: df.write().mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("schemaName.tableName") Native DataFrame Plotting# PyHyperBatch supports native plotting, allowing users to visualize data directly from PyHyperBatch DataFrames. The user interacts with PyHyperBatch Plotting by calling the plot property on a PyHyperBatch DataFrame and specifying the desired type of plot, either as a submethod or by setting the kind parameter. For instance: df.plot.line(x="category", y="int_val") or equivalently: df.plot(kind="line", x="category", y="int_val") The feature is powered by Plotly as the default visualization backend, offering rich, interactive plotting capabilities, while native pandas is used internally to process data for most plots.
